papers.title: Comment on egusphere-2026-4834
papers.summary: Abstract. Regional landslide debris inundation risk assessments are commonly constrained by scenario-based formulations that require explicit enumeration of landslide sources and runout events, limiting scalability and introducing sensitivity to subjective modelling choices. This study presents a process-based framework for regional landslide debris inundation risk assessment that employs a flux-based hazard metric to quantify probability of inundation and mean annual property loss risk. The approach builds on the Landslide Source-to-Inundation Process Model by coupling spatially distributed landslide sediment production with mass-conservative downslope routing, and converting resulting debris flux into probabilistic estimates of building damage. Risk is evaluated as a temporally integrated quantity arising from all feasible landslide sources, volumes, triggers, and return intervals, without reliance on discrete runout scenarios. We apply the method to the ~25,000 km2 West Coast region of New Zealand. Results indicate the aggregate rainfall-induced property loss corresponds to approximately 1.6 equivalent complete residential-building losses per year under present-day conditions. Under the RCP6 2081–2100 climate scenario, rainfall-induced residential APLR increases by approximately 50 %, assuming landslide sediment production increases in proportion to rainfall-induced susceptibility. Uncertainty is quantified through parametric sensitivity analysis, Monte Carlo simulation, and evaluation of topographic resolution effects. Combined uncertainty is estimated at approximately ±1.0 OOM at the 1-sigma-equivalent level for the regional 25 m model; a conservative ±1.25 OOM uncertainty is adopted for interpretation. This reduces substantially when higher-accuracy topography is employed. The framework provides a scalable and transparent basis for regional landslide risk analysis and supports risk-informed planning in landslide-prone regions.

papers.title: The Temporal Dynamics of Cryospheric and Fluvial Hazards: Deciphering the Global "Dawn Cascade
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Abstract—Himalayan and global alpine fluvial systems are highly susceptible to sudden-onset disasters, specifically Landslide Dam Outburst Floods (LDOFs) and Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs). While the spatial vulnerabilities of these systems are widely mapped via remote sensing, their temporal breach patterns remain critically understudied. This paper examines a recurring temporal phenomenon across both high-altitude Nepalese river basins and international alpine corridors over a multi-decade timeline. The data demonstrate that catastrophic containment failures disproportionately breach downstream zones between the hours of 01:30 and 09:15. By identifying the diurnal thermal and hydrostatic mechanisms behind this "dawn cascade," this study proposes a globally applicable framework for community-based early warning protocols.

papers.title: Safety performance evaluation of a gently dipping bedding slope containing multiple weak interlayers in Southwest China
papers.summary: The failure modes and safety assessment methods of gently dipping bedding slopes containing multiple weak interlayers (GBSWs) are critical issues in engineering construction. In this study, engineering geological investigations and laboratory direct shear tests on undisturbed samples were conducted to elucidate the strength degradation mechanism and the evolution of strength parameters of the weak interlayers, while finite element simulations were employed to investigate the slope failure modes. Based on the laboratory test results and numerical simulations, a back-propagation neural network (BPNN) model was developed to enable rapid assessment of the operational safety of engineering slopes. The results indicate that the shear strength of the weak interlayers decreases significantly with increasing water content, while both cohesion and the internal friction angle exhibit an exponential decay. The bedrock–overburden interface and the weak interlayers within the slope constitute unfavorable interfaces. Following excavation-induced unloading, slope deformation develops preferentially along these interfaces, resulting in an overall stepped sliding–tensile cracking failure mode. Staged excavation, together with the timely implementation of protective measures after excavation, can effectively control the factor of safety ( F s) and the maximum horizontal displacement (| U x| max ) of the slope. Comparative trial calculations showed that the 5–10–2 BPNN architecture exhibited the best performance, yielding the lowest root mean square error (RMSE) and the highest coefficient of determination (R²). For GBSWs, an analytical limit equilibrium method applicable to the engineering feasibility study and preliminary design stages, together with a predictive assessment method based on machine learning for the safe operation stage, was proposed.

papers.title: Applicability of Friction Velocity Estimation Methods in Sediment-Deposit-Induced Non-Uniform Open-Channel Flow
papers.summary: ABSTRACT Wenchuan earthquake–induced landslides generated large volumes of sediment that formed lateral sediment deposits in mountainous river channels, significantly altering flow structures and channel evolution. Under such strongly non-uniform flow conditions, accurate estimation of bed shear stress remains challenging. Because bed shear stress is difficult to measure directly in natural rivers, friction velocity is commonly used as an indirect proxy. This study conducted fixed-bed flume experiments with representative riverbank sediment deposits to evaluate six classical friction-velocity estimation methods under uniform-flow conditions and four methods—the Reynolds shear stress (RSS), turbulent kinetic energy (TKE), vertical turbulent kinetic energy (TKE w′), and logarithmic law methods—under sediment-deposit conditions. The results show that estimated friction velocity is more closely associated with turbulence intensity than with longitudinal mean flow velocity. Turbulence-based methods (RSS, TKE, and TKE w′) showed more consistent responses than the logarithmic law method under strongly non-uniform flow conditions, with the TKE method exhibiting the most stable performance across different flow zones. This study clarifies the applicability and limitations of classical friction velocity estimation methods under different degrees of flow non-uniformity, providing guidance for estimating bed shear stress and conducting sediment-transport studies.

A quantitative geophysical–geotechnical framework for slope stability analysis using electrical resistivity tomography
papers.summary: Abstract Slope instability constitutes a major constraint on infrastructure development in geologically complex and rapidly urbanizing regions such as West Java, Indonesia. Reliable slope stability analysis requires spatial characterization of subsurface mechanical parameters, including cohesion, internal friction angle, and bulk density. Conventional geotechnical investigations provide accurate point-scale data but are often constrained by high cost, limited spatial coverage, and logistical challenges. This study presents an integrated geoelectrical–geotechnical framework enabling the quantitative use of electrical resistivity for slope stability assessment. The investigation was conducted in the Padalarang District, West Bandung Regency, an area dominated by volcanic lithologies. Electrical Resistivity Tomography and Vertical Electrical Sounding were integrated with borehole logs, Standard Penetration Test data, and laboratory measurements to derive empirical correlations between resistivity and key geotechnical parameters. The results indicate a very strong correlation between electrical resistivity (ρ) and cohesion (R 2 = 0.8270), a strong correlation with bulk density (ρᵦ) (R 2 = 0.6860), and a weak correlation with internal friction angle (R 2 = 0.1780). The resistivity-derived parameters were incorporated into limit-equilibrium slope stability analysis under the specified groundwater condition. The representative resistivity-derived parameter model produced a Factor of Safety (FoS) of 2.60, while the final spatially integrated slope model yielded a minimum FoS of 1.23. These results demonstrate that electrical resistivity can provide spatially continuous, site-specific geotechnical information for preliminary slope stability assessment when calibrated and constrained by borehole and laboratory data.

Review article: Mountain flash floods: from hazard formation to disaster risk reduction pathways
papers.source: Natural hazards and earth system sciences
papers.summary: Abstract. Flash floods in mountainous regions are becoming more frequent and destructive under climate warming, yet cross-regional understanding of their triggering mechanisms, cascading impacts, and governance remains fragmented. This review synthesises 1,967 studies published during 2000–2025 to establish a globally comparable baseline of mountain flash-flood research. By integrating bibliometric and topic analyses with qualitative synthesis, we reveal pronounced geographical and thematic imbalances, with research concentrated in Europe and Asia. At the same time, many high-risk mountain regions in Africa and South America remain overlooked. Across regions, flash-flood initiation and impacts are shown to be strongly state-dependent and coupled, emerging from interactions between storm intensity, duration and spatial concentration, antecedent hydrological conditions, and hillslope-channel connectivity. This coupling helps explain why fixed rainfall thresholds are difficult to generalise and highlights the need for dynamic, multi-source early-warning approaches. Comparing evidence on early warning, structural protection, and Nature-Based Solutions, the review shows that cascading processes dominate risk management challenges. We therefore propose an adaptive governance framework that links monitoring and forecasting, spatial planning, grey-green integration, and basin-scale risk sharing under non-stationary climate conditions. Overall, this synthesis consolidates fragmented evidence into a cross-regional knowledge base to support flash-flood risk reduction in mountainous regions, where data and capacity are limited.

papers.title: Coupled Flow-Deformation Analysis of Unsaturated Slopes Subject to Wet-Induced Failures and Stabilized by Micropiles
papers.summary: Abstract Slope instability induced by rainfall infiltration and other sources of water leakage (e.g., pipeline leakage) is a major geotechnical concern, particularly in unsaturated soils, where changes in matric suction can significantly affect the shear strength and stability of the soil slope. This study investigates the hydro-mechanical response of unsaturated slopes subjected to continuous infiltration and evaluates the effectiveness of micropiles in mitigating wetting-induced failures. A two-dimensional finite element model was developed in PLAXIS 2D (V2024.1) using fully coupled flow–deformation analysis. Unsaturated soil behaviour was represented using the soil-water characteristic curve and hydraulic conductivity functions based on the van-Genuchten formulation. The numerical model was validated using field observations from the South-to-North Water transfer Project in Hubei Province, China, and later published numerical studies. Subsequently, the validated model was employed to investigate the performance of micropile-reinforced slopes under infiltration conditions. The study has shown that, under continuous infiltration, the factor of safety (FoS) of the unreinforced slope decreased significantly within 30 days, approaching imminent failure due to the loss of matric suction and a reduction in effective stress. A comprehensive parametric study was conducted to evaluate the influence of micropile position, length, inclination, and diameter on slope performance. The results demonstrated that micropile reinforcement significantly enhanced slope stability, increasing the FoS by about 20% if the most favourable pile-length configuration was adopted. The study has shown that the most effective reinforcement configuration was achieved by installing micropiles within the lower part of the slope face with lengths exceeding the slope height, with inclinations between 50° and 60° from the vertical and diameters within the range of (PL/80–PL/40). papers.title: Co-producing just sustainabilities: integrating local knowledge and geospatial analysis for climate-sensitive rural settlement planning in the East African Highlands
papers.summary: Highland rural settlements face increasing climate-related hazards, but vulnerability is shaped not only by environmental exposure but also by livelihood dependence, place-based relationships, and governance arrangements. This study examines how local knowledge and geospatial analysis can be integrated to understand rural settlement vulnerability in Rwanda’s Western Highlands. Using a concurrent mixed-methods design, we combined household surveys (n = 280), qualitative inquiry (104 participants), and GIS-based hazard assessment. Results show that landslides, floods, and soil erosion substantially affect rural livelihoods, while perceived risks correspond with spatial patterns of hazard exposure. However, continued residence in exposed areas reflects constrained adaptation choices shaped by agricultural dependence, cultural attachment, institutional arrangements, and limited relocation alternatives. The findings demonstrate that knowledge co-production can provide a basis for socially grounded climate-sensitive planning by connecting spatial evidence with community experiences and addressing questions of risk distribution, knowledge recognition, and decision-making authority.

papers.title: Navigating the Legal Architecture of AI
papers.summary: A state that ignores a 95.6% accurate landslide prediction and then invokes force majeure is not applying a legal doctrine it is abusing one. Force majeure and the Act of God defence share a single operative requirement. Machine learning has destroyed that requirement. AUC values for flood and landslide prediction routinely exceed 0.90 rendering catastrophic events institutionally foreseeable before they occur. The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) reframes the analysis. Classifying disaster-management systems as high-risk AI raises the standard of care for public authorities and makes force majeure progressively harder to sustain as a complete defence. Explainability is a due-process obligation here, not a technical amenity: communities subject to AI-driven evacuation orders hold a legitimate interest in understanding the basis for those decisions. The concern that strict liability will deter disaster-AI deployment is real and deserves a substantive answer. This chapter proposed a standards of domestic enforcement, pre-deployment sandboxes, safe harbours, and compensation funds.

papers.title: A calculation model for the loess collapse coefficient considering progressive wetting dry density and applied vertical pressure
papers.summary: Predicting wetting-induced collapse of loess requires accounting for the coupled effects of applied pressure, moisture state, and pore structure. Laboratory collapse tests were conducted on remolded Ili loess at different water contents, dry densities, and applied vertical pressures. A three-factor coupled model was developed using dimensionless pressure, degree of saturation, and void ratio. The main contribution is a continuous parameterization that allows the collapse coefficient to be calculated across the investigated soil states without independently refitting each water-content–dry-density combination. The model describes the nonlinear pressure-dependent response and incorporates moisture and pore-structure effects through saturation- and void-ratio-dependent parameters. Evaluation against the laboratory data yielded an overall coefficient of determination of R 2 = 0.783. A dimensionless wetting parameter was introduced to evaluate changes in remaining collapse potential across independently prepared moisture states within the tested range. An engineering-scale application to a 30 m loess profile predicted a self-weight collapse settlement of 3330.71 mm, compared with a reported field measurement of 3520 mm, corresponding to a relative error of 5.38%. Because some field conditions exceeded the laboratory calibration range, this comparison indicates application potential rather than general validation. The proposed formulation links routinely measured soil properties with collapse-coefficient estimation and layerwise settlement assessment.

papers.title: Reply on RC1
papers.summary: Abstract. Geo-hydrological hazards, including floods and landslides, are among the most widespread hazards and a major cause of human loss worldwide. Their impacts are shaped by meteorological forcing and by long-term changes in exposure, vulnerability, and settlement patterns. Yet robust assessments of long-term fatality trends are rare because sufficiently long, accurate, and homogeneous records of damaging events are lacking. A key unresolved question is whether the human toll of geo-hydrological events has changed structurally through time, and which climatic, socio-economic, or policy factors best explain that change. Here we show, using a unique 1950–2024 catalogue of fatal events in Italy, that geo-hydrological risk underwent a marked transition, with fatalities and fatal days declining sharply until about 1970 and then stabilising at much lower levels. This decline was driven mainly by landslides, whereas flood-related losses showed weaker long-term change. The decline was not explained by specific risk policies or management programmes, as most of it preceded their implementation. Instead, precipitation was the main climatic driver of the remaining interannual variability, particularly for floods and days with fatal events. By contrast, population and gross domestic product did not account for the long-term trends once shared temporal changes were considered. Fatal days were less overdispersed and more predictable than fatalities, suggesting that meteorological factors control more directly the occurrence of dangerous conditions than the final death toll. Fatalities, instead, depend strongly on exposure, vulnerability, timing, location, and other event-specific circumstances. Together, these findings indicate that broad socio-economic dynamics can reduce geo-hydrological mortality even as hazardous processes persist, whereas meteo-climatic conditions continue to shape year-to-year risk.

papers.summary: Abstract. We present a methodology to retrieve 3D surface displacement based on Digital Image Correlation (DIC) applied to multitemporal terrain models. Our approach has been developed to overcome the DIC limitation in the vertical component of the displacement field when horizontal shifts are larger than the grid sampling. To validate the performance, we applied the approach to two terrain models acquired over the Brienz/Brinzauls landslide, where surface displacements affect the entire slope with heterogeneous amplitudes and directions. The comparison with in-situ measurements shows that DIC can accurately retrieve horizontal and vertical displacements, providing a clear representation of the spatial extent of the mass movement, as well as an accurate distinction of the internal landslide compartments. Our results are in good agreement with those obtained using a state-of-the-art point correlation method, but require less preprocessing and computational effort. Thus, the proposed DIC strategy can be considered as a valid alternative for measuring 3D surface displacements in scenarios where multitemporal terrain models are available.

papers.title: Classification and Remote Sensing Characterization of Large Catastrophic Landslides in the Southeastern Tibetan Plateau, China
papers.summary: Large catastrophic landslides in the southeastern Tibetan Plateau are characterized by huge volumes and complex chains that frequently cause river damming and casualties. Based on field surveys, multi-temporal satellite imagery, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) deformation measurements, and meteorological and seismic records, this study classifies these landslides into three types by their initiation and disaster-chain processes: (1) rock–ice avalanche → debris flow → landslide dam; (2) debris flow → landslide dam; (3) rock avalanche → landslide dam. Representative cases illustrate the material sources, initiation settings, and downstream impacts of each type. The occurrence of such landslides is influenced by the interplay of four groups of factors: fractured rock masses and abundant loose deposits provide the material basis; high mountains and narrow river valleys provide the spatial framework for landslide evolution and promote river blockage; pronounced climatic changes provide the background conditions and may affect slope stability in glaciated areas through glacier retreat; and frequent strong earthquakes can both instantaneously trigger failure and cause cumulative damage that predisposes slopes to subsequent failures. Ongoing climate warming and repeated seismic activity are expected to increase landslide susceptibility, highlighting the urgency of multi-hazard early warning and proactive mitigation. This study supports early warning prioritization and risk governance in high-mountain valleys across the Tibetan Plateau.

papers.title: faDebrisFOAM: debris-flow modeling with coupled terrain evolution in OpenFOAM
papers.summary: Abstract. Debris-flow numerical models are widely used for hazard assessment and engineering design, yet many models still treat bed evolution in a simplified or uncoupled manner. This study presents faDebrisFOAM, an open-source depth-averaged solver developed in OpenFOAM® that couples debris-flow motion, entrainment, deposition, and terrain evolution within a finite-area framework. The model represents the mixture as an equivalent fluid of variable density and incorporates mass exchanges with an erodible bed layer through entrainment and deposition laws. The Terrain Modification Algorithm (TMA), developed in this work, updates the computational grid at each time step, allowing topographic changes to feed back directly into the governing equations and simulated flow dynamics. The model is evaluated through three applications: validation against large-scale US Geological Survey (USGS) flume experiments, testing in an idealized parabolic geometry, and application to the 2015 debris-flow event in the La Mesilla catchment in northern Chile. The solver reproduces the measured evolution of flow thickness in the USGS flume experiments with good agreement. The idealized application demonstrates that terrain evolution is not a passive output but an active control on run-out, velocity, flow depth, and volume redistribution. The La Mesilla case further shows that coupled terrain modification promotes surge self-generation, self-channelization, and channel-plug formation, which are absent or weakened when the TMA is disabled. These results indicate that coupled terrain evolution can modify flow confinement, stress distribution, and preferential routing throughout the simulation. faDebrisFOAM therefore provides an open-source framework for investigating morphodynamic feedbacks in debris-flow propagation.

papers.source: African Journal of Food Agriculture Nutrition and Development

The arrival, duration, and distribution of rainfall have traditionally provided important signals about when to prepare land, plant, weed, and harvest. But these signals are becoming increasingly difficult to read. Climate change is altering rainfall patterns, while increasingly frequent extreme weather events are making farming more uncertain. The current outlook for the October–December 2026 season brings this challenge sharply into focus. The IGAD Climate Prediction and Applications Centre (ICPAC) forecasts a wetter-than-normal season across much of the Greater Horn of Africa. The Lake Victoria Basin, which includes large parts of Western Kenya, is among the areas with a high likelihood of receiving more than 400 mm of seasonal rainfall. ICPAC reports that El Niño has developed and is expected to strengthen, while a positive Indian Ocean Dipole is also expected—climate conditions that are commonly associated with enhanced rainfall in the region, and is likely to run into February of 2027. For a farmer whose livelihood depends almost entirely on rain-fed agriculture, abundant rainfall can be a blessing. papers.title: Reply on RC2
papers.summary: Abstract. Rain-on-snow (ROS) events are a major hydrometeorological phenomenon in mountainous regions, as the combination of liquid precipitation and snowmelt enhances flood hazard. This study provides the first systematic analysis of ROS events in the French Alps at high temporal and spatial resolution, based on the S2M reanalysis (1958–2024) with an hourly time step. By combining meteorological data with an event database of torrential floods and landslides, ROS events are explicitly linked to observed impacts. Averaged over space, 5.5 ROS events occurred per year in the French Alps over 1958–2024, with a clear contrast between the more frequently affected north-western mountain ranges and the south-eastern ones. Seasonality strongly depends on elevation, with ROS events occurring mainly in winter at lower elevations and in spring at higher elevations. Impactful ROS events, associated with torrential floods or landslides, are characterized by high cumulative rainfall and long durations. Above 76 mm of cumulative rainfall, the probability that a ROS event is impactful exceeds 50 %, defining heavy-rainfall ROS events. Trend analyses reveal a marked decline in overall ROS occurrence (-22 %) between 1959–1988 and 1995–2024, primarily in spring and early summer due to a shortening of the snow season, while increases are observed in December and January as precipitation more frequently falls as rain. Heavy-rainfall ROS events show a more moderate decrease (-9 %), with declining trends in most southern mountain ranges but increases in several northern ones. They now predominantly occur in early winter at lower elevations, which are more densely populated, making them more likely to produce damaging impacts. The next step in this systematic approach would be to create a watershed-based subdivision of the French Alps to enable comprehensive hydrological analyses of ROS events.

Landslide susceptibility mapping in Mahakam Ulu, East Borneo, by using an MCDA-based factor of safety
papers.source: Journal of Infrastructure Planning and Engineering (JIPE)
papers.summary: Landslide hazard mapping has been performed in Mahakam Ulu regency in order to support disaster risk reduction and targeted mitigation efforts. The mapping was done by using topographical slope gradient, soil type, and maximum rainfall intensity data. Maximum rainfall used in this research comprises of daily rainfall data with a 20-years return period, which is assumed to be spatially uniform across the entire region. The slope parameter is calculated based on maximum rate of elevation change between a raster cell and its surrounding cells. Meanwhile, soil type is obtained by combining information from geological maps of Long Iram and Long Pahangai. The aforementioned parameters were used to calculate Factor of Safety (Fs) that indicates slope stability and were integrated using a weighted average-based multi-criteria decision analysis. The resulting Fs values are varied from 0.230-1.500. Low Fs values of 0.230 to 0.738, showing landslide-prone area, can be seen along the northern border between Long Apari and Long Pahangai districts. Areas with low Fs values are also observed along the eastern border between Long Bagun and North Borneo province, the southern part of Long Hubung, and a small area in northern Laham. The Fs values were also used to construct a landslide susceptibility map with three hazard levels: low, moderate, and high. Areas with low level of landslide hazard prevail throughout Mahakam Ulu. Nevertheless, large portion of landslide-prone areas in Long Apari and Long Pahangai point to the importance of hazard risk reduction and targeted mitigation efforts tailored for the mentioned regions.

Data were collected through questionnaires administered to 21 respondents representing 15 stakeholder institutions, and analyzed using UCINET, NetDraw, and Gephi based on degree centrality, betweenness centrality, closeness centrality, and network density indicators. The results indicate that communication, coordination, and information sharing achieved mean scores of 3.81, 3.95, and 3.75, respectively, all classified as good. Stakeholders' perceptions of the collaborative network structure reached a mean score of 4.05, indicating strong support for inter-organizational collaboration. The network analysis identified the Regional Disaster Management Agency (BPBD) as the primary operational actor, with the highest degree centrality (14) and closeness centrality (0.875), while the Regional Development Planning Agency (Bappeda) recorded the highest betweenness centrality (42.35), highlighting its strategic role in coordinating policies across institutions. A network density value of 0.543 indicates a moderately strong collaborative network, although stronger cross-sectoral integration remains necessary. papers.title: Spatial assessment of landslide susceptibility in Donomulyo based on GIS-MCDA and AHP
papers.source: Journal of Infrastructure Planning and Engineering (JIPE)
papers.summary: Donomulyo Subdistrict in Malang Regency is characterized by complex hill–coastal terrain that is increasingly pressured by tourism development, making it highly prone to landslides. This study assesses landslide susceptibility using a Geographic Information System–based Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (GIS–MCDA) integrated with the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP). Five conditioning factors—slope, rainfall, land cover, soil type, and geology—were analyzed and weighted through pairwise comparison to generate a spatial susceptibility map. The results show that most of Donomulyo lies within moderate susceptibility zones, reflecting widespread geomorphological instability and emphasizing the need for risk-sensitive land-use management. Scientifically, this research demonstrates the applicability of the GIS–AHP framework to an understudied tropical hill–coastal environment, where local-scale integration of terrain, rainfall, and land-use dynamics remains limited in existing literature. The study’s spatial outputs provide quantitative guidance for zoning, slope conservation, and community-based mitigation—actions that directly support SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), SDG 13 (Climate Action), and SDG 15 (Life on Land). By explicitly linking geospatial hazard modelling with sustainable development planning, this research advances the use of spatial analysis as a decision-support tool for disaster risk reduction and resilient regional development in Indonesia.

papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Abstract The Eastern Himalayas represent one of the world's most ecologically sensitive and dynamically evolving mountain systems, rendering them exceptionally vulnerable to contemporary climatic shifts. This study presents a comprehensive geospatial assessment of climate-induced hazards in the Papum Pare district of Arunachal Pradesh, India. Situated within the Sub-Himalayan and Lesser Himalayan zones, Papum Pare experiences extreme topographical variance, fragile geological formations and intensive monsoon regimes, culminating in acute susceptibility to flash floods, landslides and slope instability. Utilizing a multi-criteria evaluation (MCE) framework integrated within a Geographic Information System (GIS) and remote sensing environment, this research maps and analyzes hazard susceptibility across the district. Spatial parameters—including elevation, slope angle, slope aspect, lithology, soil characteristics, land use and land cover (LULC), normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and proximity to drainage networks and road corridors—were parameterized, weighted using the Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) and aggregated to generate district-wide hazard susceptibility indices. The empirical findings reveal that approximately 28% of the geographical area in Papum Pare falls under "High" to "Very High" hazard susceptibility categories, with urbanized expansion zones along river valleys and unengineered infrastructural arteries exhibiting the greatest risk profiles. The results underscore the imperative for localized climate adaptation strategies, risk-informed spatial planning and resilient infrastructure development in the Eastern Himalayan fringe. papers.summary: Regional landslide susceptibility prediction commonly treats diverse failure mechanisms as a single statistical entity, an oversimplification that fails in lithologically complex red-bed basins, where retrogressive and translational landslides follow fundamentally distinct hydromechanical laws. Here we develop a mechanism-divergent framework that integrates frequency ratio factor screening, Bayesian probability for uncertainty-aware dataset construction, and a mixture probabilistic neural network to explicitly fuse multi-modal susceptibility indices. The approach is validated in Sanshui District, a subtropical red-bed basin in China, using a 15-year multi-source inventory. Random forest and logistic regression are coupled with frequency ratio and Bayesian strategies to independently predict each landslide type. Bayesian-enhanced models consistently outperform their frequency-ratio counterparts, with Bayesian random forest achieving the highest accuracy. The mixture probabilistic neural network captures spatial heterogeneity through distance-weighted neural connections, markedly improving regional mapping and attaining an area under the curve of 90.2%, substantially higher than the 66.7% of conventional unified models. Shapley additive explanation analysis identifies lithology, annual precipitation, and road proximity as dominant controls; lithostratigraphic Groups 1, 7, 12 and 13 exhibit the highest susceptibility. This framework offers a lithostratigraphy-informed, mechanism-aware pathway for landslide risk assessment in complex soft-rock terrains.

In the V4.2 reference rerun, the Direct Insertion Method (DIM) and an algebraically equivalent internal-variable update agree to a relative L2 difference of 7.27e-16 in final effective stress sigma_zz. A separate full-history constitutive comparison covers irregular strain increments, holds, and limiting decay factors, with relative L2 differences below 6.72e-16. The results revealed distinct factor-ranking patterns between the two approaches, reflecting their different weighting philosophies. While AHP emphasized surface geomorphological controls, particularly slope, CT assigned the highest weight to transverse resistance, highlighting the influence of subsurface weathering, groundwater conditions, and rock competence on slope instability. The resulting susceptibility maps were classified into five categories and validated using landslide inventory data and Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis. The CT model achieved an Area Under the Curve (AUC) value of 0.74, outperforming the AHP model (AUC = 0.63). papers.title: Determination of Erosion Potential of Rioni River Basin Using GIS and RUSLE Model
papers.summary: This study focuses on determining the soil erosion potential within the Rioni River basin using the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) and Geographical Information System (GIS) technologies. A 90-meter resolution Digital Elevation Model (DEM) from the Shuttle Radar Topographic Mission (SRTM) was utilized to delineate the basin boundaries and hydrological network. The RUSLE model, an empirical approach, was applied to estimate the long-term average annual soil loss. Individual RUSLE factors were computed using specific methodologies: the rainfall-runoff factor (R) was derived from a linear empirical relationship based on average atmospheric precipitation (1989-2021); the soil erodibility factor (K) was calculated using the Sharpley–Williams equation, yielding a value of 0.0184 for the prevalent soil type; the topographic factor (LS) was determined using a RUSLE-adapted approach; the cover-management factor (C) was calculated using the Durigon equation from NDVI values; and the support practice factor (P) was assigned based on slope and cultivation practices. Results indicate that the R-factor ranges from 313.65 to 473.89 MJ×mm/(ha×hours), with an average of 391.02 MJ×mm/(ha×hours). The maximum LS-factor reached 7137.810. The C-factor values (0.104 to 0.769) suggest a significant risk of water erosion across the basin. Overall, the study concludes that riverbed erosion predominantly occurs in the Rioni River basin, primarily influenced by flow velocity and slope.

papers.title: Landslide Susceptibility Assessment in Badong County, Hubei Province, Based on Machine Learning and SHAP Interpretability Analysis
papers.summary: Badong County is located in the hinterland of the Three Gorges Reservoir Area and is characterized by complex geological conditions and highly rugged terrain, making landslide susceptibility assessment particularly important. Based on an inventory of 384 landslides, this study retained 11 conditioning factors and constructed a balanced dataset with a 1:1 ratio of landslide to non-landslide samples. Sensitivity analysis of 500, 1000, and 1500 m buffer distances showed only small differences in non-landslide sampling, with the 1000 m buffer retained for subsequent analysis. The dataset was evaluated using both a conventional 7:3 random training–test split and five-fold spatial block cross-validation, with the spatially independent results used as the primary basis for model evaluation. Four machine learning models, namely RF, MLP, SVM, and XGBoost, were compared. Under spatial block cross-validation, XGBoost achieved the highest mean AUC of 0.8662, compared with 0.8751 under the random split, and also showed the best overall performance among the four models. Calibration analysis further indicated good agreement between the predicted susceptibility scores and the observed landslide proportions. Bootstrap resampling was used to quantify prediction uncertainty, and the integration of susceptibility and uncertainty identified areas characterized by both high susceptibility and high uncertainty. Independent validation using spatially withheld landslides showed that the high- and very-high-susceptibility zones accounted for 29.25% of the study area and contained 71.61% of the withheld landslides. SHAP analysis indicated that elevation, distance to road, slope, and NDVI were the principal contributors to the XGBoost model output. Overall, the results provide a spatial reference for landslide susceptibility zoning, preliminary engineering-site screening, and the prioritization of field investigation and monitoring in Badong County.

papers.title: A steadily flowing glacier and no detectable precursor before the 11 October 2026 Budhi Gandaki rock–ice avalanche and flood, Nepal
papers.summary: On 11 October 2026 at about 04:20 local time, a rock–ice avalanche at the head of the Ungilung Khola, on the southern slopes of Chamar (7,165 m) in Gorkha District, Nepal, became a debris flow and flood that travelled down the Syar Khola and the Budhi Gandaki. I reconstruct the event from free satellite data (Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, Landsat 8/9, ITS_LIVE and NISAR), official records and my own reading of historical Google Earth imagery, in the four days after the event, before any clear 10 m image. Each change test is compared with a control, where possible a fake event made from images taken before the event. The change mapped at the source on 11 October happened between 6 October 10:41 and 11 October 10:42 local time. A river gauge 23 km downstream recorded no flood pulse between 5 and 11 October. On 13 October, Landsat 9 shows a 0.31 km² block of snow loss at 5,020–5,470 m on an unnamed valley glacier, absent in the fake test, and a candidate avalanche track at 6,350–6,600 m above face B; face A is unchanged. The glacier had flowed at about 60–130 m yr⁻¹ for a decade, and no speed-up or other precursor was detected. Newly public L-band interferograms from NISAR kept face B within about ±2 cm along the line of sight in every pair from May to 7 October, and showed nothing unusual on the hanging glacier above it in the pair that ended 9.5 hours before the collapse. Radar at 06:03 recorded a fresh rough surface, most likely deposit or debris-laden water, 0.5–1.5 km up the Syar Khola from its confluence with the Ungilung, where the blockage and a 1.5 km backwater were reported. The flood reached Arughat, 63 river km downstream, in at least three rises, the largest last. The source scar, volume and any chain of small lakes remain unmeasured until clearer images arrive.

papers.title: Cascading Cryosphere Hazards in a Warming Himalaya A Secondary-Data Analysis of the August 2026 Nepal–Tibet Glacier-Collapse Debris Flow
papers.source: International Journal of Sociology and Social Research
papers.summary: The glacier temporarily blocked the Lhende Khola River, then released a destructive debris flow that travelled through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli corridors into the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading in Nepal. This paper relies on secondary data from government disaster management bureaucracies and reporting from the United Nations, multilateral banks, and print and broadcast media. It focuses on the events surrounding the disaster, analysis of causal factors, casualties, damage to infrastructure and the economy, and response efforts by the government and international agencies. On August 29, 2026, the toll in Nepal was reported to be 675 dead with 2,478 missing and over 93,000 affected, while Tibet reported 7 dead and 560 missing persons. The calamity destroyed about 430 megawatts of hydropower capacity, 19 bridges, and 40 kilometres of road, while obliterating the vital Gyirong border crossing for Nepal-China trade. This paper discusses the event in the context of available scientific literature on glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) and ice–rock avalanches in High Mountain Asia, highlighting that the same Bhote Koshi corridor faced a similar transboundary glacial lake outburst event in 2016, which points to an issue of recurrent and unmitigated risk. The study finds there are still gaps in cross-border early detection, information sharing across borders, and infrastructure management based on climate risks, and gives some suggestions for governance and engineering. This study provides an early and organised description of a quickly changing disaster which will be useful for investigators, practitioners in civil defence planning, and policy-makers, but it also notes the limits of this investigation using secondary sources. papers.title: ResQNet: A Crowdsourced Disaster Preparedness and Real-Time SOS Mesh Network Using Wi-Fi Direct MANET, Delay Tolerant Networking, and Artificial Intelligence
papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: Natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods, cyclones, landslides, and wildfires frequently damage cellular towers and internet infrastructure, leaving victims unable to contact rescue teams and depriving responders of real-time situational information. This paper presents ResQNet, a crowdsourced, infrastructure-independent disaster communication system that uses Wi-Fi Direct-based Mobile Ad Hoc Networking (MANET) and Delay Tolerant Networking (DTN) to relay SOS alerts between nearby smartphones without relying on cellular or internet connectivity. Each smartphone in the network functions simultaneously as a sender, relay, and store-and-forward node: SOS packets, tagged with a unique identifier, timestamp, GPS coordinates, hop count, and time-to-live (TTL), are propagated hop by hop until they reach an internet-enabled gateway device or a rescue authority. Duplicate packet suppression and TTL-controlled flooding are used to keep the network efficient under heavy load. ResQNet further incorporates artificial intelligence for emergency severity classification, location-based clustering of victims, accessibility analysis, and hotspot identification, together with voice-triggered SOS activation for hands-free operation. A web-based dashboard visualizes live SOS alerts, victim clusters, and priority levels on a map to support rescue coordination. Simulation-based evaluation of packet delivery ratio, latency, and message loss indicates that the proposed architecture can sustain reliable emergency communication even when conventional networks fail, offering a scalable and low-cost foundation for future disaster-response systems.

Ground surface displacement data from the Slumgullion landslide, Hinsdale County, Colorado, November 2010 to March 2024
papers.summary: We monitored ground surface displacement at as many as three locations on the Slumgullion landslide located in Hinsdale County, Colorado between November 23, 2010 and March 21, 2024. Displacement at the ground surface was measured approximately daily (the time of record varied throughout the monitoring period) at locations upon the upper (E1), middle (E2), and lower (E3) parts of the landslide along its left lateral (southeastern) boundary using electronic cable extension transducers (extensometers; Celesco PT8101 model) with manufacturer-stated ±0.7 mm accuracy (extensometer_data.csv). Sensors and their anchors were installed above the ground surface on galvanized steel posts partly driven by hand into the ground on opposite sides of a strike-slip fault forming the landslide’s left margin. Posts were driven into the ground at angles such that the extension cable was oriented parallel to the fault and measured the length of cable extending from the sensor housing approximately parallel to the direction of landslide movement. Sensors had approximate maximum ranges of 1524 mm and were episodically reset to lower values by moving extension cables to newly driven anchor posts located closer to the sensors. However, sensors sometimes over-ranged and failed, likely providing inaccurate data when the maximum range was reached until failure occurred. Additional errors and omissions in the data likely resulted from problems with the solar- and battery-powered dataloggers including power loss, loading of rain, snow, and ice on extension cables and anchor posts, frost heaving, animal activity, and other factors. Erroneous data are excluded from the data provided here when that error was clear during inspection; however, it is almost certain that some error remains. papers.summary: Malawi’s urban areas are increasingly vulnerable to climate-related disasters, including flooding, landslides, and extreme winds, while conventional infrastructure struggles under these pressures dueto outdated designs, limited maintenance, and poor climate adaptation. This study aims to examine how Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG)-aligned green infrastructure (GI) can strengthen urban resilience in resource-constrained Malawian cities, with a focus on Blantyre and Zomba. A qualitative, exploratory study was conducted using systematic document analysis of secondary sources, with thematic analysis applied to identify patterns in climate risk, governance constraints, and lessons for context-appropriate green infrastructure strategies. Findings show that GI interventions, including urban wetlands, permeable pavements, slope vegetation, and tree planting, offer significant environmental, social, and governance benefits: they reduce flood and landslide risks, improve waterquality, support biodiversity, create green jobs, enhance public health, and foster community inclusion, while strong governance ensures sustainability through institutional accountability, integrated planning, and transparent financing. A key limitation of this study is the absence of primary stakeholder interviews, which limits direct insights into municipal implementation challenges. Future research should engage local planners and communities to validate and extend these findings. This study provides guidance for policymakers, urban planners, and development partners on designing and implementing ESG-aligned green infrastructure strategies that reduce disaster risks and promote inclusive urban development. papers.title: An ensemble JCHAIDStar framework for improved landslide susceptibility prediction using Bagging and Random Subspace techniques
papers.source: Journal of Science and Transport Technology
papers.summary: This study developed a landslide susceptibility map for the mountainous area of northern Vietnam, located within the administrative boundary of the former Ha Giang Province and now under Tuyen Quang Province, to support the identification of landslide-prone areas and disaster risk reduction. The input data included a landslide inventory of 963 locations and 13 conditioning factors representing topographic, hydrological, geological, climatic, and human-related conditions. The dataset was divided into training and validation subsets using a 70:30 ratio. Four models, including Bagging-based JCHAIDStar (Bag-JCHAIDStar), Random Subspace-based JCHAIDStar (RSS-JCHAIDStar), Deep Neural Network (DNN), and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), were developed and compared using model performance metrics and Taylor diagram analysis. The results show that Bag-JCHAIDStar achieved the best overall performance, with AUC = 0.988 for the training dataset and AUC = 0.950 for the validation dataset. On the validation dataset, this model also obtained ACC = 88.7%, Kappa = 0.760, and RMSE = 0.291, indicating good classification and generalization capability. The validation of the landslide susceptibility zoning map using the Frequency Ratio method showed that the very high susceptibility class had the highest landslide proportion, accounting for 52.11% of the total landslide pixels and reaching the highest FR value of 1.817. These results suggest that the Bag-JCHAIDStar model can provide useful support for landslide susceptibility assessment, disaster risk reduction, and sustainable land-use planning in mountainous areas.

papers.title: Toward a Modern Risk and Resilience Data System in Sweden: Diagnostic and Recommendations
papers.summary: Like many European countries, Sweden faces a growing array of natural hazards, including floods, storms, wildfires, landslides, and climate-related events, as well as their potential cascading effects. Sweden has an advanced and well-developed disaster risk management framework, characterized by continuous improvement and guided by the national risk assessment, the national climate adaptation strategy and the total defence system. This report assesses the current state of Sweden’s disaster risk data system and identifies pathways for developing a modern unified risk and resilience data system. The findings reflect stakeholder engagement across government agencies, research institutions, and private sector actors, as well as a review of existing data flows, institutional arrangements, and technical capacities. This report is accompanied by an international review, which provides a comprehensive assessment of global practices in disaster damage and loss data systems, drawing on a wide range of country experiences and established methodologies to identify key principles for effective system design. It highlights that successful systems are anchored in a clearly defined purpose aligned with user needs, as this determines critical features such as information scope, data granularity, accessibility, and update frequency. Disaster data systems should be developed incrementally, starting with a narrow scope that uses existing capacities and institutional structures rather than creating wide-ranging parallel systems that attempt to serve many purposes at once. Over time, a narrow system can be adjusted and expanded as needs evolve.

papers.summary: Rain classification consists of several categories of rain, such as light rain, moderate rain, and heavy rain. Therefore, to cover the weaknesses of the KNN method, an optimization is needed for the K value using the Particle Swarm Optimization method so that the accuracy results obtained are optimal..PSO will optimize the selection of K values by initializing the respective K value particles used for KNN classification, then updating the position and velocity based on PBest and GBest. The process will be repeated in certain iterations until the criteria are met and will produce an optimal K value. From the K value by testing using the confusion matrix obtained an accuracy of 99.88%. From optimizing using PSO on KNN, getting a better time in selecting K values is 3 minutes 52 seconds, whereas without optimizing using PSO on KNN, you get approximately 5 minutes. This proves that PSO optimization on KNN can provide good time efficiency in selecting the most optimal K value

papers.title: The Terra Nova Condominium: a critical evaluation of the population resettlement policy after the 2011 extreme-rainfall in nova Friburgo, Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil
papers.summary: This study examines the socio-spatial impacts of the Terra Nova Condominium, a housing complex in Nova Friburgo (RJ), established after the extreme rainfall-induced landslides and natural disaster of 2011. The relocation of displaced residents highlighted various vulnerabilities, exacerbated over time by inadequate planning and socio-spatial segregation. The findings reveal that prolonged residency in the complex correlates with greater dissatisfaction concerning building security and infrastructure. Additionally, the study identifies how the original community’s socio-cultural ties were severed, impeding adaptation. The residents, many from rural backgrounds, faced difficulties adjusting to urban life, missing their previous environments' social and economic benefits. This research parallels other global post-disaster resettlements, emphasizing the systemic flaws of top-down housing policies prioritizing profit over social needs, thereby intensifying the marginalization of vulnerable populations. The conclusion calls for more participatory approaches in housing policies, which include residents in decision-making processes, thus fostering resilience and reducing social vulnerability.

papers.title: Target-focused supervision and fine spatial evidence improve sparse landslide detection in remote-sensing imagery
papers.summary: Introduction Regional landslide screening must retrieve sparsely annotated failures among visually similar terrain while limiting false review candidates. Small scars can lose spatial detail during downsampling, and extensive background regions can dominate semantic supervision. Methods We developed the Sparse Landslide Detection Transformer (SLD-DETR) by adapting RT-DETRv4. It combines scale-guided focused distillation (SGFD), which concentrates teacher–student alignment near annotated landslides; high-resolution scale-aware supervision (HRSS), which supervises stride-4 features; and stride-4 decoder memory (S2-Mem), which exposes fine spatial features to query selection and cross-attention. We evaluated five independent training seeds on a source-scene-disjoint 6:2:2 split of the Multi-Scale Landslide Dataset (MSLD). For screening performance, confidence thresholds were calibrated on validation to a false-positive rate of no more than 0.10 false positives per image (FPPI), then frozen for testing. We also assessed zero-shot transfer to LRSTTC-New. Results On the held-out MSLD test split, SLD-DETR achieved a mean average precision of 58.07 ± 1.10 % across IoU thresholds 0.50–0.95 (mAP@50:95) and 63.43 ± 1.23 % mAP@75, compared with 53.90 ± 0.96 % and 58.34 ± 2.65 % , respectively, for RT-DETRv4-S. At the validation-calibrated operating points, test miss rate was 15.82 ± 2.18% for SLD-DETR and 18.63 ± 0.99% for the baseline. Under zero-shot cross-region transfer, all detectors degraded substantially; SLD-DETR had the highest AP within the RT-DETRv4 family, while RF-DETR-S performed best overall. Discussion The coordinated modules improved box-level screening on the evaluated source-disjoint MSLD split. SGFD and HRSS are training-only, whereas S2-Mem remains at inference and adds approximately 0.06 million parameters. Runtime and memory costs increase with image resolution.

Child health challenges in the 2025 Sumatra flood and landslide: Lessons for disaster risk reduction and emergency response
papers.source: Jàmbá Journal of Disaster Risk Studies
papers.summary: In late 2025, catastrophic floods and landslides struck Sumatra, Indonesia, causing widespread destruction and nearly 1200 fatalities. Children were among the most severely affected, experiencing acute health problems, disruptions in essential healthcare services and significant psychosocial distress. This essay employs an evidence-informed analytical approach, integrating contemporaneous official reports, available scientific literature, international disaster risk reduction (DRR) frameworks, Emergency Medical Team (EMT) standards and the authors’ direct field experience during the disaster response. The disaster is examined across the disaster management cycle, including prevention, mitigation, preparedness, emergency response and recovery, to identify gaps between established child-centred disaster management principles and their practical implementation. The analysis demonstrates that, despite national policies and international guidance, implementation was inconsistent. Many children experienced preventable illnesses, interruptions in chronic medical care, inadequate continuity of paediatric healthcare and unmet psychosocial needs because of coordination challenges, limited child-focused preparedness and fragmented service delivery. The findings highlight that integrating child-centred DRR principles with specialised paediatric emergency training, strengthened EMT deployment, continuity of essential child health services, coordinated mental health support and multisectoral collaboration can improve disaster preparedness and emergency response. The lessons learned provide practical guidance for strengthening child-centred DRR, improving emergency response systems and informing policy development that better integrates child protection and paediatric healthcare into all phases of disaster management.

papers.title: An overview of discrete element modeling for slope stability

papers.summary: The paper examines the main directions of the impact of natural hazards on the landscapes of Okriba and their role in the structural and functional transformation of landscapes. The study analyses the natural conditions of the territory, the spatial distribution patterns of hazardous processes, and their interrelationships with relief, geological structure, hydrological regime, soil, and vegetation cover. Particular attention is paid to landslides, erosion, debris flows, and flood processes, as well as to the potential impacts of extreme climatic events. One of the key areas of the research is the assessment of the interaction between natural hazards and anthropogenic pressures. The landscapes of Okriba are considered as geographical systems undergoing continuous transformation under the combined influence of natural and anthropogenic factors. The paper also assesses the vulnerability of different landscape types to natural hazards and identifies the main directions for enhancing their resilience. Based on the findings of the study, several characteristic landscape settings were identified as particularly susceptible to the development and spatial occurrence of landslide processes. These include river-valley slopes; highly dissected hilly and low-mountain terrain; slopes adjacent to transportation infrastructure, particularly roads; and anthropogenically modified slopes in the vicinity of settlements. The results of the study can be applied to the rational use of Okriba’s natural resources, spatial planning, environmental management, and the development of measures aimed at reducing natural hazard risks.

papers.title: LIA-adaptive Goldstein phase filtering for improved InSAR displacement estimation in landslide-prone terrain
papers.summary: Abstract Reliable InSAR-based monitoring of ground deformation is often hindered by atmospheric disturbances and phase noise, particularly in regions with rugged topography and high vegetation cover. However, limited work has explored integrated phase filtering and atmospheric correction strategies in complex, landslide-prone terrains like Mizoram, India. This study proposes an enhanced methodology combining a Modified Goldstein phase filter and Atmospheric Phase Screen (APS) removal to improve Line of Sight (LOS) displacement estimation. Mizoram, characterized by frequent landslides and challenging climatic conditions, provides an ideal testbed to evaluate these improvements. Twenty Sentinel-1 SAR images (10 ascending, 10 descending) were processed using SRTM DEM-based co-registration, with corrections addressing height distortions and DEM voids. This study modifies the standard Goldstein filter that incorporates Local Incidence Angle (LIA) information to enhance phase unwrapping stability, combined with Atmospheric Phase Screen (APS) removal applied before phase filtering. Furthermore, an ensemble learning framework using a Random Forest regressor was employed to model and refine time-series displacement trends. The proposed method constrained phase values within a range of -3 to 3 radians, improved displacement map interpretability, and achieved a LOS displacement of±80 mm/month. Validation against ground-collected levelling survey data showed a strong correlation of 76% (n=20 levelling points, p < 0.01) with the modified Goldstein filter applied LOS displacement values, as against 46% (n=20 levelling points, p < 0.05) for the normal Goldstein phase filter applied LOS values. Additionally, 5-fold cross-validation of the Random Forest ensemble model yielded training and testing R² values of 0.892 and 0.856, respectively, confirming the reliability of the displacement estimates.

papers.title: SBAS InSAR, UAV, and Numerical Modeling of Slope Instability in Tbilisi, Georgia
papers.summary: The Vere River basin in Tbilisi, Georgia, experienced a major cascading landslide–flood disaster in June 2015, emphasizing the need to evaluate the present stability of slopes adjacent to the former source area. This study combines small-baseline InSAR (SBAS), RTK-UAV photogrammetry, COSI-Corr image correlation and LS-RAPID numerical modeling to investigate whether the slope remains active and how it responds to changing pore-pressure conditions. Analysis of 109 ascending Sentinel-1 acquisitions acquired between April 2022 and October 2025 revealed persistent positive line-of-sight deformation across the investigated slope. Independent UAV/COSI-Corr analysis identified horizontal displacements of approximately 0.05–0.09 m over 149 days, exceeding the empirical relative displacement detection threshold of 0.0235 m. The measured displacement direction broadly follows the downslope and structural orientation, although its angular offset suggests that the movement is influenced by a combination of topography, bedding, fractures, and heterogeneous slope materials rather than a single planar control. LS-RAPID simulations further showed a nonlinear response to increasing prescribed pore-pressure ratio. Together, the observations indicate that the slope has not fully stabilized after the 2015 event and continues to undergo slow deformation while remaining sensitive to hydrological conditions. This is particularly important for Tbilisi because renewed slope instability in the Vere valley could interact with the confined river corridor and urban infrastructure, increasing the potential for cascading impacts.

papers.title: Extreme Rainfall-Induced Landslides on 1 June 2025 in Southern Assam, Northeast India
papers.source: Journal of the Geological Society of India
papers.summary: ABSTRACT In the early hours of 1 June 2025, a series of landslides occurred in the Rajpur Village of southern Assam, Northeast India, following incessant rainfall due to early onset of the Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM). The landslides occurred almost simultaneously along the partially weathered hillslopes composed primarily of matrix supported gravels, between 03:00 and 03:30 IST. These were preceded by an extreme rainfall pulse of 230 mm recorded at 02:30 IST which is part of a cumulative total of 458.8 mm over the previous three days in the area. The landsides caused grievous injuries to a few people and damaged number of dwelling units with consequent displacements. Post disaster site investigation and first-hand accounts suggest an extreme rainfall triggered shallow landslide mechanism in play when saturation in the porous rock and soil mass exceeded threshold. In this report we present a preliminary assessment of the rainfall event and physical site factors leading to the landslides on this particular date. The good correlation observed here between rainfall record and occurrence of landslides provides an important case study to work out a regional threshold for rainfall triggered landslides in the foreland fold belt region of Northeast India. This will further contribute towards developing a region-specific landslide early warning system in a scenario of changing monsoonal regime.

papers.title: Safety and Resilience in Slope Engineering Design for New Buildings under Extreme Rainstorm Climates
papers.summary: The safety of construction slopes holds significant importance in engineering and architecture, with the lack of resilience against extreme weather conditions being particularly critical. This paper systematically examines the fundamental flaws in traditional design theories regarding the limitations of compression-shear stress paths and the assumption of constant soil parameters. It delves into the systemic vulnerabilities in resilience across the entire lifecycle caused by operational supervision gaps and post-event regulatory gaps in the current construction system. Additionally, it reveals the consequences of mechanistic isolation between structural support and ecological protection, as well as the oversimplified engineering approach resulting from outdated drainage system standards, through real-world disaster case studies. Based on this, this article proposes a theoretical revision direction for constructing a tension shear fluid-solid coupling unsaturated soil mechanics system, explores a differentiated zoning control mechanism based on quantitative risk analysis (QRA), and integrates digital Bayesian pre-evaluation methods with on-site observations. The research aims to provide rigorous theoretical support for the disaster-resistant design of high-risk building slope engineering, and promote the transformation of slope engineering from static defense to a dynamic resilience management paradigm throughout its lifecycle.

papers.title: Integrating rockfall and debris flow monitoring and early warning networks into risk mitigation and emergency planning in Brescia Province, Italy
papers.summary: Italy is highly exposed to rapid landslides such as rockfalls and debris flows, which strongly affect mountain communities, infrastructure, and land management. Mitigation strategies traditionally rely on structural measures, including active stabilization works and passive protection systems, but their effectiveness depends on site-specific geological and geomorphological conditions and event magnitude. In this context, monitoring and Early Warning Systems are increasingly recognized as essential tools to complement structural interventions and reduce loss of life. Recent advances in sensors, communication technologies, and data processing have made local and territorial landslide Early Warning Systems more feasible, although their implementation remains challenging due to false alarms, threshold definition, validation procedures, and the need for continuous maintenance. This paper presents three case studies from the Province of Brescia, Northern Italy, showing how monitoring and alarm systems can be integrated into risk mitigation and land management. The first concerns a rockfall-prone site where unusual trajectories and high bounce heights required a combined system of flexible barriers, a multipurpose interception net, impact sensors, and traffic-light-based warning devices. The second describes a debris-flow Early Warning Network based on continuous meteorological and hydrometric monitoring, event-triggered wire sensors, and rainfall thresholds. The third illustrates an integrated multi-hazard network that monitors rockfalls, debris flows, and floods at the municipal scale. Together, the case studies highlight the value of combining structural and non-structural measures to support emergency planning and improve territorial safety.

papers.title: Neural network derived landslide risk assessment system
papers.source: Journal of Environmental Engineering and Landscape Management
papers.summary: Landslide is a frequent form of natural disaster in a tropical region such as Western Sarawak, Malaysia, and the occurrences are commonly associated with the wet season. Contemporarily, Landslide Susceptibility Map (LSM) produced by machine learning models are used to assess the landslide risk. However, LSMs are known to have spatiotemporal issues, where recent changes in the spatial data used as inputs in the models are not reflected in the LSMs, causing unjustified landslide susceptibility score in certain areas. The same issue was also observed in Western Sarawak’s LSM. Thus, this study was focused on transforming the Artificial Neural Network model used developed the region’s LSM into a set of equations that can be used as a landslide risk assessment system. The new system was determined to be highly accurate with a score of 1 for both Area Under the Curve score, and recall.

papers.source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.summary: EarthTrends is a multi-source Earth Observation framework developed to assess the impact of permafrost thaw on land degradation across the Arctic. Rapid warming is accelerating processes such as thermokarst formation, vegetation change, slope instability, and risks to infrastructure, yet monitoring these dynamics requires integrating heterogeneous satellite datasets and analytical methods. EarthTrends addresses this challenge through a modular Python architecture that fuses long-term satellite archives (Landsat), Copernicus Sentinel data, MODIS time series, and high-resolution optical imagery with advanced statistical and artificial intelligence approaches. The framework quantifies ecosystem change using multi-sensor vegetation index time series analysed through linear regression, Mann–Kendall trend tests, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models to detect non-linear dynamics and anomalies. Thermokarst features are automatically mapped from high-resolution imagery using a U-Net deep learning segmentation model. Land degradation susceptibility is further evaluated by modelling soil freeze–thaw cycles as proxies for slope instability and landslide potential. Environmental indicators are intersected with socio-economic datasets to estimate impacts on settlements and infrastructure. Preliminary results show that the thermokarst detection component is operational and capable of identifying surface subsidence features, while freeze–thaw analyses reveal anomalies linked to areas of increased degradation risk. Vegetation trends highlight spatially heterogeneous ecosystem responses to warming across the Arctic. Overall, EarthTrends demonstrates the feasibility of an integrated, scalable framework for monitoring permafrost-driven environmental change and its societal implications. The system is intended for pan-Arctic application and will be released as an open-source tool to support research, monitoring, and decision-making related to climate-induced land degradation.

papers.title: Failure mechanism and dynamic process of the Jinping high-position and long-runout landslide in the Wumeng mountainous area, China, on 8th February 2025
papers.summary: The Wumeng Mountain area is characterized by complex geological conditions and is prone to high-position, long-runout landslide–debris flow chains. This study integrates field investigation, remote sensing interpretation, InSAR monitoring, laboratory tests, and numerical simulation to reveal the deformation evolution, genetic mechanism, and kinematic process of the landslide. The results show that the controlling factors can be stratified into two levels. At the geological level, the anti-dip fragmented rock mass with interbedded hard and soft strata constitutes the primary internal cause of slope instability, while the steep-upper and gentle-lower topography provides the morphological precondition for the transformation of the sliding mass into a debris flow. At the rainfall level, continuous infiltration significantly reduces slope stability and acts as the key triggering factor. Initial deformation appeared in 2014 and accelerated continuously after 2020, eventually leading to failure, with unstable rock masses still remaining at the rear scarp. Simulation results show that the entire process lasts about 50 s, with a maximum velocity of 48 m/s and a maximum accumulation thickness of 23 m, accompanied by progressive fragmentation of the rock mass. Such landslides share similar disaster-prone characteristics, which can provide references for the early identification of potential landslide hazards in the region.

Traditional Monte Carlo-based random field methods are computationally expensive, while passive sampling-based machine learning models often suffer from inefficient data utilization. This study develops a physics-guided data-driven learning framework with active learning (PGDAL) for spatially variable slope stability analysis. The framework integrates MNMM-based high-fidelity simulations, active learning-based sample selection, and CNN/U-Net surrogate models. Spatially varying soil properties are represented as image-based inputs, while F s , displacement fields, strain fields, and CSS information obtained from MNMM simulations are used as learning targets. Four query strategies, including LCUS, margin sampling, entropy sampling, and maximum standard deviation sampling, are compared to evaluate their effects on model performance. The proposed framework enables multi-response prediction by learning the nonlinear relationship between random field inputs and slope responses, and further identifies smooth CSS through predicted deformation fields. Results demonstrate that PGDAL achieves higher prediction accuracy and faster convergence than passive sampling while requiring fewer high-fidelity samples. The proposed framework provides an efficient surrogate modeling approach for intelligent slope stability analysis considering spatial variability.

However, the repeated extraction of multiple extra-thick coal seams induces complex overburden responses, and the effects of mining sequence on slope deformation and stress evolution remain insufficiently understood. To address this issue, two physical similarity models representing upward and downward mining sequences were established. A non-contact digital image correlation (DIC) system, together with an embedded stress-monitoring system, was employed to monitor the evolution of displacement and stress fields within the overburden. The results show that the mining sequence governs slope deformation by controlling the propagation of mining-induced disturbances and the subsequent redistribution of stress within the interburden strata. Under the upward mining sequence, the disturbance generated by extraction of the lower seam propagated toward the slope and was further intensified by subsequent extraction of the upper seam, resulting in a maximum vertical displacement of 2.22 m and pronounced stress concentration in the middle and lower parts of the slope. In contrast, the downward mining sequence was associated with earlier stress redistribution toward the cemented backfill, which contributed to mitigating the disturbance caused by subsequent extraction of the lower extra-thick seam. Consequently, the maximum vertical displacement decreased to 1.76 m, representing a 20.5% reduction compared with the upward mining sequence, while cumulative overburden subsidence and stress concentration were effectively mitigated. These findings demonstrate that mining sequence plays a critical role in the mechanical response of open-pit slopes and provide mechanistic insights into the optimization of mining strategies for cemented backfill mining beneath open-pit highwalls.

papers.summary: Wildfires are among the most destructive natural phenomena on Earth, and their frequency, intensity, and duration have dramatically increased in recent decades due to the accelerating impacts of climate change. The combination of rising global temperatures, decreasing humidity, prolonged droughts, and altered precipitation patterns has created an environment that is increasingly conducive to large-scale fires. This book chapter comprehensively examines the interconnections between climate change and wildfire dynamics, emphasizing the role of both natural and anthropogenic drivers. It provides an overview of how global warming reshapes vegetation structures, soil moisture content, and atmospheric circulation patterns—factors that collectively amplify the probability and severity of wildfires. Furthermore, the chapter explores the feedback loop between wildfires and climate change, where fires not only result from climate alterations but also contribute to them through the release of massive amounts of greenhouse gases and aerosols. These emissions further intensify global warming, creating a vicious cycle that threatens ecological stability and human well-being. Regional case studies and global data analyses illustrate how fire regimes have shifted across continents, including in boreal forests, tropical rainforests, and Mediterranean-type ecosystems. The environmental consequences of intensified wildfires extend beyond immediate destruction. Long-term effects include soil degradation, biodiversity loss, water contamination, and severe disruptions to carbon sequestration processes. In addition, wildfires have substantial socio-economic implications—causing property losses, displacement of communities, and public health crises due to smoke exposure and poor air quality. To address these escalating challenges, the chapter underscores the urgent need for integrated and adaptive fire management strategies. This includes the implementation of sustainable land-use policies
