papers.title: Impact of Rainfall Infiltration on Groundwater Seepage under the Effect of Urban Construction in Shanghai
papers.summary: Abstract Groundwater seepage is influenced by various anthropogenic factors during urban construction, among which subsurface structures and surface hardening are two key factors. This study employed numerical simulations to investigate the impacts of rainfall infiltration on groundwater seepage under the effect of urban construction. A numerical model was established to predict groundwater level (GWL) in the phreatic aquifer (Aq0), incorporating the actual distribution of impervious surfaces and subsurface structures for a representative urban area in Shanghai. The model accounted for land surface conditions through rainfall infiltration coefficients, while subsurface structures were parameterized using equivalent hydraulic conductivity ( K eq ) derived from effective medium theory. Validation results show that the model achieved a maximum error of only 1.7%, demonstrating reliable performance in predicting groundwater seepage. There is 23.23% area with GWL declining more than 0.4 m in the actual scenario with 93% impervious surface hardening comparing without surface hardening. Prediction scenarios with varying reduction rates of impervious surface compared with the actual scenario ( R a ) were conducted to investigate the impact of surface hardening on GWL. The results indicate average GWL of the study area presents exponential decay with the impervious surface ratio. Further, the variations in GWL of Aq0 were investigated by reducing hardened surfaces in different locations with the same R a . As the proportion of underground structures in the reduced impervious surface increases, the area with the same increment of GWL decreases. Prioritizing low impact development in areas with lower subsurface structure density can significantly enhance the efficiency of groundwater recharge by rainfall infiltration.

papers.title: Evolution Process and Failure Mechanisms of Rockfalls Revealed by the Integration of Ambient Seismic Noise and Multi-Source Monitoring Data
papers.summary: Abstract. Rockfall hazards are characterized by their sudden occurrence, complex evolutionary processes, and the difficulty of identifying reliable precursory signals for early warning. Understanding their failure mechanisms and precursory characteristics remains a key scientific challenge in geohazard research. In this study, the Mogangling high-elevation rockfall, triggered by the 5 September 2022 Luding earthquake, was selected as a representative case. Based on long-term in situ observations, we developed an integrated analytical framework that combines ambient seismic noise with hydro-mechanical multi-source monitoring data to investigate the evolution and failure mechanisms of rainfall-induced rockfalls. A rockfall event detection method based on the short-term average/long-term average (STA/LTA) algorithm was established to identify rockfall events, while relative seismic velocity changes (dv/v) were extracted from ambient seismic noise interferometry to characterize temporal variations in the internal state of the rock mass. These results were further integrated with rainfall, hydrological observations, and slope stability analyses. During the monitoring period, a total of 329 rockfall events were identified and classified into three categories:single-trigger events, short-duration event clusters, and continuous rockfall sequences. Rockfall activity was strongly associated with rainfall but exhibited pronounced nonlinear, stage-dependent, and time-lagged responses. The dv/v measurements were highly sensitive to internal structural changes within the rock mass, showing significant anomalies approximately 2 h before failure and a rapid decrease of about 3 % during the collapse, indicating the transition from progressive damage accumulation to catastrophic failure. papers.title: A scenario-based economic valuation framework for ecosystem service benefits of biochar-mediated soil erosion control
papers.summary: Abstract This study quantifies the gross ecosystem-service benefits of biochar-mediated soil erosion control across climate, agricultural, and water-system pathways, while treating runoff reduction as a non-monetised hydrological co-benefit. Soil erosion is a major driver of land degradation, with global losses exceeding billions of tonnes annually and affecting approximately 24% of European land. Meta-analytical evidence indicates that biochar application reduces soil erosion by 16% and surface runoff by 25% on average, with stronger effects observed in erosion-prone environments. Using this evidence, three baseline erosion scenarios were evaluated. Under low, moderate, and high baseline erosion scenarios, central gross benefits were €2.80, €9.33, and €24.19 ha⁻ 1 yr⁻ 1 , respectively. Monte Carlo analysis yielded median total values of €2.95 (95% uncertainty interval: €1.36–€7.48), €9.85 (€4.54–€24.92), and €25.52 (€13.81–€56.21) ha⁻ 1 yr⁻ 1 , respectively. These estimates exclude biochar production, transport, and application costs and therefore represent gross co-benefits rather than net economic returns. Mediterranean experiments reported erosion reductions of up to 67%, substantially above the global mean, illustrating the strong context dependence of biochar responses but not providing a basis for regional economic extrapolation. The results identify soil erosion control as a potentially measurable co-benefit of biochar deployment across climate, agricultural, and water systems. The framework provides a transparent basis for future site- and region-specific valuation while explicitly accounting for uncertainty in biophysical and economic parameters.

papers.title: Development of an IoT-Based Hydrological Parameter Monitoring System Using an Eco-Hydrology Approach to Support Sustainable Water Resources Management
papers.summary: Reliable, site-specific hydrometeorological observations are essential for supporting eco-hydrological analysis and water resources management. This study developed and evaluated a low-cost Internet of Things (IoT)-based Mini-Automatic Weather Station (Mini-AWS) integrating an ESP-12E/F microcontroller, temperature and humidity sensors, a tipping-bucket rain gauge, local data storage, wireless communication, and a solar-assisted battery system. Field evaluation was conducted during August 2026 using observations from the Indonesian Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG). Analysis of 43,967 synchronized temperature and relative humidity pairs yielded a temperature RMSE of 1.066 °C and MAPE of 2.550%. The uncalibrated humidity measurements exhibited an RMSE of 10.881 %RH and a positive measurement bias. A second-order polynomial humidity calibration model was selected using temporally separated training and validation blocks and evaluated on 10,052 internal test observations. Calibration reduced humidity RMSE from 11.500 to 2.848 %RH and MAPE from 17.165% to 3.938%, although residual autocorrelation and heteroscedasticity remained. The correction also reduced the RMSE of AWS-derived Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD) from 0.3701 to 0.1668 kPa and improved agreement with BMKG-derived operational VPD categories from 45.09% to 81.86%. Initial volumetric calibration of the tipping bucket yielded 0.5084 mm/tip, while 15 additional controlled-flow experiments produced a mean resolution of 0.544 mm/tip; natural-rainfall accuracy was not independently validated. The prototype acquired meteorological data during a 31-day deployment using a solar-assisted 2500 mAh Li-ion battery, although battery-voltage accuracy and energy savings were not independently verified. The dashboard incorporated VPD, empirical Ivanov Potential Evapotranspiration (PET), and Rain-Free Days indicators as preliminary eco-hydrological interpretation tools. papers.title: Failure Mechanism of a Rainfall-Induced MSE Wall Embankment Revealed by Two-Stage Numerical Back-Analysis
papers.summary: Rainfall infiltration is one of the main causes of embankment failure because it changes the engineering properties of soil and reduces slope stability. Conventional stability analyses commonly assume uniform soil conditions, which may not represent the actual field condition after prolonged rainfall. This study investigates the failure mechanism of an MSE wall embankment at Kedungmlati 2 Overpass, Mojokerto–Kertosono Toll Road, using a two-stage numerical back-analysis. Laboratory tests were performed on embankment soils under different degrees of saturation (Sr = 50%, 62.5%, 75%, 87.5%, and 100%) to determine the corresponding engineering properties. The numerical analyses were conducted using the finite element method implemented in PLAXIS 2D. Stage 1 evaluated six numerical models with uniform saturation conditions throughout the embankment. None of these models reproduced the observed failure mechanism. Stage 2 introduced a non-uniform saturation distribution to represent localized rainfall infiltration along the embankment slope The modified model successfully reproduced the observed failure surface. The results demonstrate that the non-uniform saturation scenario adopted in Stage 2 provided a closer agreement with the observed failure mechanism than the uniform saturation scenarios evaluated in Stage 1. In this scenario, a saturated near-surface zone and a relatively unsaturated embankment core were assigned as part of the back-analysis procedure to reproduce the observed failure pattern. The proposed rehabilitation measures further increased the safety factor from 1.085 to 1.765, effectively restoring embankment stability. These findings suggest that considering spatial variations in the degree of saturation can provide a more representative prediction of rainfall-induced failure mechanisms than assuming a uniform saturation distribution. The novelty of this study lies in the proposed practical back-analysis approach, which combines a non-uniform saturation

papers.title: Evidence of vertical soil hydraulic heterogeneity regulating hydrothermal simulations in Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau wetlands
papers.summary: Abstract. Alpine wetlands on the Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau host vertically structured and highly contrasting pore systems that fundamentally shape land and atmosphere exchanges, yet their hydraulic expressions and process implications remain poorly quantified. This study provides the first process based and depth resolved characterization of these layered pore structures using soil physical analyses and laboratory evaporation experiments. The derived Clapp–Hornberger parameters reveal coherent hydraulic contrasts, with surface layers dominated by macropore connectivity and showing high θs and Ks and low b that promote rapid drainage and evaporation, mid layer domains with lower θs and Ks and larger b that enhance retention in finer pores, and deeper layers that act as stable and persistent storage reservoirs. These properties together generate a vertical regime of rapid near surface drainage, delayed mid layer release, and long lasting deep moisture storage. When implemented in Noah-MP, this hydraulic stratification systematically altered water and energy partitioning during wet and dry periods and showed that vertical hydraulic heterogeneity rather than a single layer parameterization governs the timing and magnitude of evaporation and heat fluxes. These findings provide the first quantitative evidence that pore scale structure regulates profile scale hydrothermal responses in Qinghai-Tibetan Plateau wetlands and establish a physically grounded basis for representing vertically heterogeneous hydraulic processes in land surface models.

papers.title: Changes in groundwater-surface water interactions following two centuries of irrigation practices and groundwater use in the Upper Ganges-Yamuna interfluve, North India
papers.summary: Abstract. The Indo-Gangetic Basin (IGB) is a global hotspot for groundwater overexploitation. Previous studies have shown that groundwater levels initially rose due to enhanced recharge following the construction of irrigation canals, but subsequently declined as agricultural, municipal, and industrial abstractions intensified. However, the relative impacts of separate recharge and abstraction components (precipitation, canal leakage infiltration, irrigation return flow, and irrigation, municipal and industrial abstraction), remain unclear, as do the effects on groundwater-surface water interactions and environmental flows. This study therefore aims to quantify spatio-temporal changes in groundwater recharge and abstraction components over the past two centuries and assess how these changes have impacted groundwater–surface water interactions in the Upper Ganges–Yamuna interfluve in northern India. Groundwater model simulations indicate that canal water infiltration following canal construction after 1830 boosted recharge, but since the 1970s increased abstractions have lowered groundwater tables and reduced river exfiltration. Currently irrigation accounts for roughly 85 % of abstractions, with municipal (15 %) and industrial (< 1 %) uses accounting for much smaller shares. From around 2000, abstraction lowered groundwater tables to such an extent that local rivers likely shifted from draining to infiltrating conditions. As a result, groundwater–surface water interactions in local rivers may have fundamentally changed. This shift threatens environmental river flows, degrades surface water quality by limiting wastewater dilution, and harms groundwater quality where polluted river water infiltrates the aquifer, posing risks to both ecosystems and human health. Although both the Yamuna and the Ganges show reduced groundwater exfiltration, they are not (yet) infiltrating.

From Hydroclimatic Extremes to Recharge Planning: A Multi-Evidence Decision-Support Framework for the Multan-Lodhran Aquifer, Punjab, Pakistan
papers.summary: Groundwater depletion in the Multan-Lodhran aquifer is intensifying as pumping expands faster than replenishment. This study explicitly separates two evidence types: (i) published baseline endpoints, which are recalculated here for transparent growth and water-budget indicators, and (ii) analyses performed in the present manuscript, comprising area-weighted GRACE/GRACE-FO storage residuals (2002–2024), a five-model bias-corrected NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 precipitation ensemble, precipitation-extreme diagnostics, and GIS-based managed aquifer recharge (MAR) screening. From the published baseline, built-up land increased from 346 to 417 km2 between 2000 and 2023; municipal wells rose from 16 to 92 by 2020; the urban-central groundwater decline was about 0.57 m yr−1; and the recalculated recharge-to-abstraction ratio declined from 1.15 in 2006 to 0.72 in 2020 and 0.58 in the 2045 projection. The new GRACE residual analysis indicates persistent regional storage loss, but the GRACE/GRACE-FO mission gap and residual surface-water contributions preclude treating the full-record slope as a homogeneous groundwater-depletion rate; pre-gap Theil–Sen slopes were −0.42 and −0.48 cm yr−1 for pre- and post-monsoon conditions. Under far-future SSP5-8.5, annual precipitation increases by 21.88%, while winter precipitation declines and monsoon/post-monsoon rainfall and upper-tail extremes intensify. These climate results describe precipitation opportunity rather than simulated groundwater recharge. GIS screening identifies low-slope alluvial areas with surface-water access as candidate investigation zones, not validated MAR sites. The framework is therefore intended for planning: site-specific hydrogeology, source-water quality, infiltration performance, and monitoring must be demonstrated, and recharge measures must be implemented alongside abstraction control.

papers.title: Post-wildfire changes to water quality: a review with implications for harmful algal blooms and reservoir resiliency
papers.summary: Abstract Wildfires wreak havoc on both urban and natural ecosystems and are expected to worsen under future climate conditions. Wildfires have the potential for long-term impacts on the health of downstream reservoirs. This study seeks to compile current literature worldwide regarding impacts of wildfires on reservoir water quality, with a special focus on the implications for harmful algal blooms. The overarching purpose was to fully understand wildfire impact on aquatic health and identify key gaps in research that are needed for accurate management of reservoirs. Due to changes in watershed conditions post-wildfire (mainly temperature, light, and nutrient dynamics), burned waterbodies are more susceptible to blooms in the months to years following a wildfire, with forested areas having recorded algae in burned waterways as high as 5–71× than that of unburned and simulated forested reservoirs showing up to 3× the peak chlorophyll-a values as their simulated unburned counterparts. Changes in algae are mainly attributed to changes to soil properties, increased nutrient loads, and increased light availability and temperatures caused by burning of surrounding vegetation. Factors that influence algae can be short-term, such as light limitation from smoke and large influxes of nutrients and metals, or longer-term, such as changes to canopy cover, legacy nutrients in sediments, surrounding runoff, and sediment chemistry. These external changes can influence harmful algae blooms (HABs) through alteration of bloom timing, extent, and community composition. There is still a need for longer-term studies of nutrient and algal dynamics, as most studies are limited to monitoring algae immediately following a wildfire. It is essential that reservoir managers anticipate how aquatic ecosystems are likely to respond to higher frequency and severity of wildfires and how their management strategies will need to be adapted.

Based on the hourly monitoring data from 2020 to 2025, the multi-time-scale analysis framework of ‘hour-day-month-aggregation period’ was constructed, and the time-lag cross-correlation was adopted. The vertical lag response law of soil moisture at different depths to rainfall was systematically quantified. The core innovations are as follows: methodologically, the study achieved precise identification of the time lag between rainfall and soil water; in theory, the coupling relationship between ‘rainfall intensity, infiltration depth and lag response period’ has been quantitatively elucidated; in practice, a vegetation management plan has been proposed that prioritises herbs and shrubs, whilst requiring careful selection of tree species. The results indicate that the lag response period for the shallow layer (0–28 cm), middle layer (28–100 cm) and deep layer (100–255 cm) are 3–4 h, 23–24 h and 6–7 days, respectively; as rainfall intensity increases from light to heavy rain, the lag response period in the deep layer shortens from 9 to 3 days. This study provides a scientific basis for research into the ‘rainfall intensity-infiltration-root system’ coupling mechanisms on the Loess Plateau and for the construction of sustainable ecosystems.

papers.summary: Petroleum contamination can alter particle contacts and fluid distribution, thereby affecting the engineering behaviour of soil. This study investigates oil-contaminated silty sand under natural moisture conditions using unconfined compression, static-water disintegration, falling-head permeability, SEM–EDS, NMR, image analysis, and apparent water-droplet contact-angle tests. The UCS decreased continuously from 31.95 kPa at 0% oil content to 12.63 kPa at 12%, representing a 60.5% reduction. In contrast, resistance to static-water disintegration increased with oil content: the uncontaminated specimen disintegrated within approximately 50 s, whereas the 8% and 12% specimens remained largely intact after 24 h. Hydraulic conductivity and time to first water discharge showed non-monotonic responses, reaching measured maxima of 13.52 × 10 − 3 cm/s and 120 s, respectively, near 5% oil content. This response is regarded as an empirical turning feature under the present test conditions rather than a universal threshold. The microscopic results suggest changes in local particle-surface appearance, fluid-relaxation behaviour, visible interparticle spaces, and composite-surface wetting response. Overall, oil contamination weakened compressive resistance while delaying static-water disintegration, and the hydraulic response resulted from the combined effects of initial water entry, fluid distribution, local flow-path changes, and possible preferential flow.

papers.title: Load Transfer and Negative Skin Friction of Pile Foundations in Collapsible Loess: Field and Numerical Study
papers.summary: Abstract Wetting-induced collapse of loess can trigger significant negative skin friction (NSF) along pile shafts, leading to adverse effects on pile load transfer and bearing performance. Field static load tests were first conducted to investigate the load-transfer behavior of single piles under natural moisture conditions. Subsequently, in-situ immersion tests were performed using a combined wetting method involving an immersion pit and seepage holes to examine NSF development under wetting conditions. A three-dimensional numerical model was also established to interpret the pile‒soil load-transfer mechanism observed in the field tests and to conduct parametric analyses. The results indicate that the three test piles exhibit typical friction-pile behavior under natural moisture conditions. Wetting-induced staged collapse of the surrounding loess resulted in segmented NSF development and multiple neutral points along the pile shaft. Pre-wetting of the surrounding soil significantly intensified NSF development and altered the axial force distribution. The numerical simulation reasonably captured the general trends of load transfer and NSF evolution observed in the field tests. The findings provide insight into the mechanism of pile-soil interaction and NSF development in collapsible loess under wetting conditions.

papers.title: Assessing the Transferability of a Basin-Scale HEC-RAS Rain-on-Grid Model Across Independent Hurricane Events
papers.summary: Reliable simulation of hurricane-induced flooding is challenging because rainfall–runoff generation, river flow, and floodplain inundation interact across large basins. This study evaluated the cross-event transferability of a fully distributed, two-dimensional HEC-RAS Rain-on-Grid (RoG) model for the Tar–Pamlico River Basin in eastern North Carolina. The model integrates terrain, land cover, soil-infiltration properties, and gridded rainfall within a hydrodynamic framework. It was calibrated using Hurricane Matthew (2016) and was independently validated for Hurricane Florence (2018) using unchanged parameters. Performance was assessed against observed discharge, flood depth, and inundation extent. Across streamflow gages, calibration yielded Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) values of 0.73–0.99, coefficients of determination (R2) of 0.78–0.99, and ratios of root mean square error to observation standard deviation (RSR) of 0.10–0.51. Independent validation produced NSE values of 0.63–0.98, R2 values of 0.81–0.99, and RSR values of 0.15–0.60, indicating consistent performance despite differing hurricane rainfall and flood responses. The validated model was subsequently applied to a 500-year design storm to generate basin-scale flood-hazard information. The findings demonstrate that a calibrated basin-scale RoG model can retain useful predictive capability across independent hurricane events and support flood-hazard assessment and emergency planning in hurricane-prone river basins.

papers.title: Multidimensional spatiotemporal differentiation and driving mechanisms of soil erosion in a mountainous small watershed: an ST-TransUNet-R framework
papers.summary: Soil erosion threatens ecological security and water conservation in mountainous small watersheds. To improve pixel-level assessment under complex terrain and incomplete multi-source raster inputs, we developed ST-TransUNet-R, a deep-learning framework that integrates a ResNet-50 encoder, a Transformer module, a joint-validity mask, and masked mean squared error loss. The framework was applied to the Xikouwai Small Watershed upstream of the Miyun Reservoir for five assessment years between 2005 and 2020 and achieved R² = 0.87, RMSE = 2.08, MAE = 1.15, and PBIAS = − 3.13%. Multidimensional analysis showed that the 600–900 m elevation band contained 48.0% of the eroded area, whereas zones above 1100 m produced disproportionately high soil loss per unit area. Slopes > 35°, vegetation cover < 30%, unused land, and skeletal soils were consistently erosion-sensitive. SHAP analysis identified slope as the dominant predictor, followed by slope length and vegetation cover, indicating that terrain-controlled runoff concentration and surface protection jointly shaped spatial erosion heterogeneity. These findings provide a high-resolution basis for prioritizing erosion-control measures in mountainous water-source protection areas.

papers.title: Recharge Performance of Pond-Based Managed Aquifer Recharge in the Ramganga Basin
papers.summary: Groundwater underpins India's water and food security but faces growing stress from overexploitation and climate change. This study evaluates the hydrologic performance of small-scale, pond-based Managed Aquifer Recharge (MAR) interventions implemented under government development programs, in the context of India's plan to construct 14 million additional recharge structures. Focusing on the groundwater-stressed Ramganga basin, the study draws on three years of participatory monitoring of 23 recharge structures. Using topographic surveys, staff gauge installations, daily water-level records maintained by trained community members, and water-balance methods, 236 recharge events were captured and associated recharge volumes quantified. While the structures demonstrated utility in recharging groundwater, performance remained below potential with a consistent declining trend. The ratio of recharge volume to pond storage averaged 1.75 in 2023 but fell to ~0.8 in 2024-25, far below values of 5-12 reported in a nearby MAR pilot. Substantial variability was observed across structure types and seasons.Declining recharge rates were linked to siltation, inadequate maintenance, and hydrogeological constraints. Pond water availability (~140 days per season) was not the primary constraint; instead, low infiltration rates mostly below 40 mm day⁻¹ emerged as the dominant limiting factor. High evaporation losses (~28% of pond storage) further reduced effective recharge. These findings highlight the need for performance-based MAR planning, integration with watershed measures, regular operation and maintenance to manage siltation, context-specific designs particularly for multipurpose ponds and participatory monitoring to build local ownership and capacity.

papers.title: Soil Water Infiltration Under Bare Soil and Maize Straw: A Field Comparison of a Double-Ring Infiltrometer and a Rainfall Simulator
papers.summary: Soil water infiltration (SWI) is central to hydrology and erosion assessment, but the measurement method and surface condition may affect the rates obtained. We compared a double-ring infiltrometer (DRI) with a rainfall simulator (InfiAsper) on a Dystric Acrisol with a sandy clay loam A horizon, under bare tilled soil and under maize straw. InfiAsper applied five rainfall treatments of equal erosivity, combining intensities of 44.6–75.0 mm h−1 with durations of 106–38 min, on four to five plots per treatment and surface. DRI tests were carried out in the same fields (22 under bare soil, 13 under ground cover) and analysed as an independent group. We (i) determined the final infiltration rate (SIR_f), (ii) compared DRI with InfiAsper, and (iii) evaluated the Kostiakov–Lewis, Horton and Philip models. Under bare soil, InfiAsper means ranged from 21.6 to 37.7 mm h−1 and the DRI mean was 86 mm h−1. A planned contrast between DRI and the mean of the five InfiAsper treatments gave a DRI/InfiAsper ratio of 1.80 (95% CI 1.00–3.23; p = 0.049); with the 20 tests of at least 15 readings, it was 2.13 (1.22–3.71). Under ground cover, InfiAsper means ranged from 15.4 to 26.3 mm h−1 and the ratio was 0.65 (0.36–1.18) with all 13 tests and 1.73 (0.93–3.22) with the five tests that ran for at least 75 min. The ratio tended to be larger on bare soil than under ground cover, depending on which ground-cover tests were used. The intensity–duration combination did not significantly affect InfiAsper SIR_f. papers.summary: Understanding soil water content dynamics under saline conditions remains a major challenge for effective soil and water management in agricultural systems. This study aimed to optimize the correction of soil water content measurements obtained from gypsum blocks under the combined effects of salinity and matric suction using Response Surface Methodology (RSM). Soil samples were collected from agricultural fields in Guangdong Province, China, representing three distinct soil textures: sandy loam, clay, and clay loam. papers.title: Advancing hydraulic conductivity estimation in the Permo-Triassic Sherwood Sandstone Group using borehole NMR logging
papers.summary: Abstract The Permo-Triassic Sherwood Sandstone Group is an important aquifer in the United Kingdom (UK) for groundwater and geothermal energy applications. Hydraulic conductivity ( K ) is essential for understanding groundwater movement, contaminant and heat transport in aquifers. Pumping test and borehole nuclear magnetic resonance logging (BNMR) were conducted in three boreholes drilled into the Sherwood Sandstone to determine K . BNMR provides information on the water-filled porosity and pore space geometry, and compared to conventional methods, it is an effective way to estimate K at a high vertical resolution. Schlumberger-Doll Research (SDR) and Timur-Coates (T-C) were used to estimate K using the standard empirical constants initially developed for petroleum reservoir applications. K SDR and K T-C were upscaled to the larger volume represented by K pumping for comparison. Both the standard SDR and T-C equations underestimated K by at least two orders of magnitude because of the limited transferability of their empirical constants to shallow groundwater systems, as they were derived for petroleum reservoir rocks rather than near-surface materials. The fits between the K SDR , K T-C and K pumping were optimised using a semi-constrained least-squares approach to obtain a set of site-specific parameters for the Sherwood Sandstone Group. The new K SDR and K T-C estimates, based on site-specific parameters, are within an order of magnitude of the K pumping . This study presents the first reported SDR and T-C constants for the Sherwood Sandstone Group, which may be used to estimate a more reliable NMR-derived high-resolution hydraulic conductivity in other locations where this formation is present.

papers.summary: Abstract. Subsurface stormflow (SSF) is a dominant process in the generation of runoff in many catchments. However, the mechanisms by which new event water triggers the activation and release of stored pre-event water are not well understood. To identify the flow paths and mechanisms governing SSF generation, we conducted a controlled sprinkling experiment using deuterium- labeled water alongside time-lapse electrical resistivity tomography (ERT), groundwater monitoring and soil core sampling at two trenched hillslopes in the Black Forest, Germany. Water was applied for three hours, with the supply switching to deuterated water halfway through the experiment. Both hillslopes responded rapidly, with event runoff coefficients of approximately 0.6, and tracer breakthrough occurred at the trenches within 7–18 minutes of application, even at depths greater than 70 cm. However, post-irrigation soil cores detected the tracer only in the uppermost 20 cm of the soil matrix, where approximately 45 % of the labeled water remained stored. Time-lapse ERT revealed that the wetting front was largely confined to the upper 0.2–1.5 m; meanwhile, the deeper, near-saturated zone exhibited negligible resistivity change despite sustained lateral discharge as measured at the trenches. Together, these observations suggest the presence of a dual-domain flow system, whereby a small proportion of event water bypasses the matrix via vertically and laterally connected preferential pathways. Meanwhile, the majority of SSF consists of pre-event water, which is mobilized by pressure-driven (piston) displacement within the saturated zone. Subsequent natural rainfall remobilized the stored tracer, raising the cumulative recovery rate to approximately 30 % within one month, thereby confirming the soil matrix to be both a sink and a delayed source of event water.

This review synthesises literature published primarily between 2015 and 2025, organising the evidence within a processing–structure–property framework that connects raw material selection and calcination conditions through hydration chemistry and microstructural evolution to mechanical and durability performance. papers.source: The Canadian Journal of Chemical Engineering
papers.summary: Abstract Natural gas hydrates naturally occur in pores of porous media. This study presents the first systematic investigation of methane hydrate formation in sub‐millimetre silica particles (0.4 and 0.7 mm) and larger sizes (1, 2, and 3 mm) as benchmarks. The combined matrix (0.4–3 mm) allows comprehensive evaluation of saturation, particle size, and amino acid effects with sodium dodecyl sulphate (SDS). Results show liquid‐phase saturation significantly affects gas storage capacity, with storage volume growing linearly as saturation increases. Particle size dominates kinetics by altering pore structure. The 3 mm system shows the fastest kinetics, reducing T90 by 30% and 57% versus 2 and 0.7 mm systems, respectively. However, the highest storage density occurs in 0.7 and 2 mm systems (157.38 and 151.63 V/V), exceeding the 3 mm system (149.70 V/V). Thus, a trade‐off exists between kinetic acceleration and ultimate storage capacity. Smaller sizes (≤1 mm) show hindered mass transfer due to poor pore connectivity, capillary force suppression, and sand bed migration. Conversely, larger sizes (≥2 mm) promote liquid migration by stabilizing pore structure, enhancing formation efficiency. The synergistic interaction between amino acids and SDS depends on hydrophobicity. When combined with SDS, less hydrophobic methionine (M) and valine (V) form ternary composite micelles. M + SDS enhances storage capacity by 26.7% by lowering critical micelle concentration, while V + SDS increases permeability by 52.3% via hydrogen bonding interference. Highly hydrophobic leucine (L) competes with SDS for gas‐water interface adsorption sites, causing an 8.3% storage capacity decrease for L + SDS and loss of nucleation advantage.

This study aims to develop a method for scaling the water retention curve and hydraulic conductivity based on the Brooks–Corey equation using minimal field data. Using the transfer matrix method, combined with the boundary conditions, the recursive relationship of the amplitude vector between the media layers is established, and the influence of the thermal-hydromechanical multi-field coupling on the seismic response of the site is systematically studied. The findings indicate that the vertical displacement amplification coefficient of the site is, in general, greater than that of the horizontal direction, with a maximum ratio of up to 36.04, and the peak value mostly occurs at incident angles less than 3° (θ is ≤ 3°). The soil structure has a significant effect on the propagation of seismic waves: Case1 (homogeneous) displacement response is gentle; Case2 (upper soft and lower stiff) fluctuates markedly at incident angles of less than 3° (θ is ≤ 3°); and Case3 (upper stiff and lower soft) is relatively stable. The parameter sensitivity analysis shows that the change of groundwater level (Case2, +384.08 % ) has the most significant influence on the displacement response, followed by the phase delay time of heat flux (Case2, +344.49 % ) and the thickness of the first layer of unsaturated soil (Case2, +335.34 % ), while the influence of Kelvin medium temperature (Case2, +64.04 % ) and thermal conductivity (Case2, +14.11 % ) is relatively limited. It shows that the amplification effect of soil conditions and thermodynamic environment on seismic response is much higher than that of thermal conductivity. In engineering practice, systematic and coordinated measurement and comprehensive analysis of soil physical parameters should be carried out to effectively control the risk of structural damage under earthquake action.

papers.summary: In this study, a total of 98 comprehensive 3D parametric finite element (FE) analyses were carried out to investigate the effect of normalized water table depth (dw/B) and relative density (Dr) of the soil beneath the footing on the ultimate bearing capacity (qult), pressure-settlement (σ-s) response, correction coefficient (cw), critical failure surface depth ratio (dc/B), and failure mechanism of a fully-rough strip footing on sandy soil. Seven different Dr values, ranging from 10% to 80% and thirteen different dw/B values, ranging from 0 to 2 as well as fully-dry condition, were preferred. The FE analysis results demonstrated that qult and cw values, and stiffness of the σ-s responses increased with increasing dw/B ratios until reaching the dc/B value. Beyond this threshold, the obtained values coincided with those corresponding to fully-dry condition. It was observed that groundwater position and the Dr of the soil significantly affected the geometry and dimension of the failure surface. Furthermore, new semi-empirical equations were proposed for predicting dc/B and cw values considering internal friction angle, dw/B, effective and saturated unit weight values, showing good agreement with the findings of the FE analyses.

Study on the Mechanical Behaviour of Unsaturated Silty Sand and Pavement Response Under Moisture Variations
papers.summary: Drainage has been widely adopted in pavement structures. Due to drainage, wetting and drying, subgrade soils may be subject to conditions ranging from saturation to partial saturation (unsaturated). Particularly, unsaturated soil exhibits matric suction in contrast to saturated soils. Matric suction can impact the mechanical response of subgrade soils. Thus, it is significant to clarify the effects of subgrade moisture variations on unsaturated soil behaviour and resulting pavement response. In this study, constant water content triaxial tests and the axis translation technique were employed to investigate the shear behaviour of unsaturated silty sand under single- and multistage loading. The multistage involved drying, wetting and free drainage stages. The shear behaviour and resilient response were demonstrated to reveal the effects of moisture variations in terms of shear strength and unloading modulus. The tests showed that peak shear strength generally demonstrated an increasing trend with a decrease in moisture content (about 20% at the confining pressure of 25 kPa), and the unloading modulus increased by about 126% at 25 kPa. Based on multi-layered elastic analysis, the effects of moisture variations on pavement response were also investigated as a representative. Maximum tensile/compressive strain, subgrade deformation and distress life were simulated. This study will help to extend the understanding of effects of dynamic moisture variations on unsaturated subgrade soils and support pavement drainage design.

papers.title: Modelling temperature-dependent hydraulic conductivity function of rooted soils
papers.summary: The performances of vegetated soil infrastructures (e.g., landfill covers, soil slopes and green roofs) are likely influenced by the temperature effects induced by decomposition of municipal solid waste, solar radiation, high air temperature and underground power cables. However, the dual effects of temperature and roots on soil hydraulic conductivity function (HCF) have remained poorly understood. In this study, temperature-controlled simplified evaporation experiments were conducted to measure soil water retention curves (SWRCs) and HCFs of rooted soils for temperature range between 24 and 54℃. Based on RT-SWRC model considering the physical occupancy of roots in pores (R) and temperature effects (T), a nonisothermal HCF model (i.e., RT-P model) was proposed by incorporating root-induced pore rearrangement (P). Furthermore, RT-P model was compared with Mualem’s model (i.e., RT-M model). Results indicated that saturated hydraulic conductivity (Ks) and unsaturated hydraulic conductivity (Ku) were increased by the roots. As the basis to develop RT-P HCF model, RT-SWRC accurately captured the temperature effects on SWRCs of both bare and rooted soils. For shrub-rooted soils in this study and grass-rooted soils from the literature, RT-P model provided a more accurate prediction for HCF than RT-M model under different temperatures, due to consideration of root-induced pore rearrangement.

papers.title: MF6PQC v1.0: coupling MODFLOW 6 and PhreeqcRM for variable-density reactive transport with evolving porosity and hydraulic conductivity
papers.summary: Abstract. Geochemical reactions can alter groundwater flow by changing solution density and porous-medium properties. Representing these feedbacks requires consistent exchange of chemical states and physical properties between reaction, flow, and transport calculations. We present MF6PQC v1.0, a Python framework coupling groundwater flow and transport in MODFLOW 6 with geochemical reactions in PhreeqcRM. MF6PQC updates solution density and converts mineral-volume changes into changes in porosity, hydraulic conductivity, and diffusion coefficients. It supports three schemes for coupling transport and reactions while retaining existing flow and geochemical model-building workflows. Comparisons with two established reactive transport models showed agreement in component transport, mineral reactions, and the evolution of porous-medium properties. An idealized evaporating salt-lake model reproduced density-driven circulation and evaporite zonation. In a heterogeneous evaporite-leaching aquifer, dissolution concentrated flow along preferential pathways, and density feedback strengthened this redistribution. MF6PQC provides configurable coupling schemes and property relationships for examining these interactions in groundwater reactive transport.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are prevalent geological hazards in mountainous and hilly regions, posing significant threats to human lives, property, and infrastructure, especially when external factors such as heavy rainfall elevate the risk of occurrence. In recent years, the rapid development of remote sensing technology, geographic information system, and big data analytics has enabled the establishment of landslide databases and the refinement of landslide hazard assessment methodologies, opening new avenues for disaster prediction and prevention research. This study focuses on the probabilistic hazard assessment of rainfall-induced landslides, using the heavy rainfall event in Nanping City, Fujian, in 2019 as a case study. The absolute probability of landslide occurrence was quantified by integrating machine learning models with Bayesian probability theory. To analyze their contributions to landslide hazard, the study comprehensively considered nine key factors: elevation, slope angle, slope aspect, topographic wetness index, fault distance, rainfall amount, topographic position index, land cover, and stratum. The findings reveal that rainfall intensity is the primary trigger for landslides. However, the occurrence of landslides also depends on the combined influence of topography, geology, and human activities rather than rainfall alone. Building on these insights, this study extends the established landslide probability assessment model to a wider region. And simulating landslide occurrence probabilities under various rainfall scenarios. This approach confirms the strong correlation between rainfall and landslides while offering scientific support for emergency management and disaster warning systems. The research provides a robust foundation for disaster prevention and control in mountainous areas, infrastructure planning, and the development of emergency response systems, particularly by refining landslide prediction models that account for multiple factors. papers.title: Landslide susceptibility modelling in Cianjur Regency using landslide numerical risk factor
papers.summary: Cianjur Regency was often hit by landslides. In 2022, this regency was affected by landslide, leading to several civilian deaths, injuries, along with damaged houses and infrastructure. To minimize the impact, determining landslide susceptibility level was proven to be an essential step in maximally plan- ning disaster management. Therefore, this study aimed to develop landslide susceptibility model in Cianjur Regency using the Geographic Information System (GIS). The landslide susceptibility model was based on Landslide Numerical Risk Factor (LNRF) method using spatial data consisting of historical landslides, the Digital Elevation Model (DEM), geology, soil types, land cover, rainfall, and earthquakes in Cianjur Regency. The accuracy of model was tested using the ROC-Curve method with a value of 0.845 being considered very good. The result showed that most of areas in Cianjur Regency had moderate and high levels of landslide susceptibility, with a percentage of 40% and 46%, respectively. Areas with high level were mostly found in the southeastern part of Cianjur Regency, moderate was evenly distributed, while low levels were in the northeastern and coastal areas.

papers.summary: Rainfall-induced landslides threaten communities and transportation corridors in data-scarce mountainous regions, where the spatial representation of rainfall and the construction of non-landslide samples can strongly influence susceptibility estimates. This study develops a reproducible GIS-machine learning framework for Hoa Binh, northern Vietnam, using 182 catalogued landslide locations (from an original 184-record catalogue after excluding two boundary records lacking complete predictor coverage), six environmental variables, and CHIRPS-derived rainfall indicators. Five models-ANN, random forest, Extra Trees, LightGBM, and XGBoost-were evaluated using a stratified 70:30 split, five-fold cross-validation, and ten independent pseudo-absence realizations. LightGBM achieved the highest mean AUC (0.686 ± 0.050), closely followed by random forest (0.681 ± 0.039), Extra Trees (0.675 ± 0.037), XGBoost (0.674 ± 0.046), and ANN (0.656 ± 0.043). Model ranking varied among realizations, demonstrating non-negligible sampling uncertainty. Final susceptibility surfaces were therefore generated as pixel-wise mean probabilities across the ten realizations, accompanied by spatial uncertainty maps. The framework shows that robust regional screening depends not only on algorithm choice but also on transparent sampling, validation, and interpretation of satellite-rainfall limitations.

papers.summary: Abstract Separated analyses are widely used to evaluate the stability of slopes after rainfall and earthquakes. However, the combined impact of rainfall infiltration and earthquake shaking on slope stability remains insufficiently studied. Therefore, a unique closed-form analytical solution to calculate the factor of safety (FS) for homogeneous unsaturated slopes under combined seepage and seismic forces has been proposed by modifying the conventional Bishop’s method. The two-dimensional seepage pattern was considered to capture rainfall infiltration, while pseudo-dynamic forces at each failure slice accounted for earthquake shaking. Further, an analytical search method was developed to locate the critical slip surface. Additionally, a coupled hydromechanical finite-element model was used to analyze rainfall-induced seepage, deformation, and stress redistribution. The resulting slope condition was further evaluated under seismic loading to represent rainfall–earthquake effects without implying full two-way coupling between infiltration and earthquake shaking. All these newly proposed methodologies were applied to the 2014 Malin landslide in Maharashtra, India, to replicate the landslide mechanism and identify root causes to show the application of proposed analytical solutions. A comparison with field observations and literature demonstrated that both the analytical and numerical models realistically represented the Malin landslide. Further, the proposed analytical model was validated against a numerical analysis of a real earthquake-induced landslide. The models accurately reproduced the onset, failure zone, and progression of instability over time. The present study provides the application of new analytical solutions for practical landslides, additionally offering a reference for prevention and evacuation plans.

papers.title: Multiobjective Optimization of Landslide Rheological Parameters Based on Random Forest and Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II
papers.summary: Abstract Rheological parameters (e.g., pore pressure coefficient r u and dynamic friction angle ϕ ) are necessary input for landslide runout evaluation. However, due to high randomness of initiation, propagation, and accumulation, it is impossible to directly measure rheological properties. This study proposes an optimization method for calibrating landslide rheological parameters based on random forest (RF) and Nondominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm II (NSGA-II). Firstly, a dynamic numerical model of landslide is established using three-dimensional model DAN (DAN3D). Then, the lateral accumulation width and the longitudinal runout distance at different spatial locations across the deposit are integrated to calibrate the rheological parameters. Next, the NSGA-II algorithm is employed to obtain the Pareto solutions of rheological parameters by minimizing the prediction errors of lateral and longitudinal runout characteristics at each location. To avoid extensive repetitive DAN3D simulations within NSGA-II, RF-based surrogate models are established to estimate the lateral and longitudinal runout characteristics at different spatial locations. The final optimal rheological parameters are objectively selected from Pareto solutions by the entropy weight method (EWM). Finally, the proposed approaches are illustrated and validated using two landslides that occurred in Gansu Province, China. Results indicated that rheological parameters optimized by the proposed approaches not only can accurately characterize the endangered area of historical events, but also provide reasonable forward prediction of runout behavior of similar landslide events with desired accuracy. RF surrogate models can remove the computational burden within NSGA-II. Integrating both the lateral accumulation width and longitudinal runout distance into the calibration of rheological parameters can improve the prediction accuracy of landslide endangered area.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslide hazards along the Banihal–Ramban corridor of the Jammu–Srinagar National Highway (NH-44) represent a critical geoenvironmental challenge in Northwestern Himalaya, where active tectonics, fragile lithology, steep terrain, and increasing extreme precipitation interact with intensive infrastructure development. This technical note presents a focused analysis of flash floods and landslides of April 20, 2025, examining their triggering mechanisms, cascading geomorphic processes, and impacts on transportation infrastructure and settlements. Historical landslide records (1990–2025) and regional hydroclimatic observations are incorporated to contextualize the event within evolving patterns of hazard frequency and anthropogenic slope modification along the NH-44 corridor. The April 2025 disaster resulted from the localized high-intensity precipitation, which elevated pore-water pressures, reduced slope stability, and triggered multiple failures in structurally weakened rock formations. Results highlight a transition from isolated slope failures toward compound and cascading hazard scenarios involving flash floods, debris flows, and infrastructure disruption. The study underscores the increasing vulnerability of this strategic Himalayan lifeline. It emphasizes the need for geologically informed engineering design, improved drainage management, and integrated early warning strategies to enhance long-term resilience.

papers.title: Numerical Simulation of Landslide-Generated Waves in Reservoirs Using a Coupled SPH-DCDEM Method
papers.summary: Abstract Landslide-generated waves occur when sliding masses impact the water surface, potentially posing significant hazards to nearby areas. This study utilizes the smoothed particle hydrodynamics–distributed contact discrete-element method (SPH-DCDEM) coupling module within DualSPHysics to simulate landslide-generated waves in reservoirs, where the SPH method models the fluid flow and the DCDEM method captures the dynamics of the granular landslide mass. The accuracy and effectiveness of the SPH-DCDEM method in simulating landslide-generated waves are validated using two physical model experiments of subaerial landslide-generated waves. Using a simplified representation of a reservoir bank deposit at the RuMei (RM) Hydropower Station in China, this study conducts an in-depth analysis elucidating the key parameters that control landslide-generated waves in reservoirs. It is found that landslide thickness and landslide entry velocity are the primary controlling factors for two-dimensional granular landslides. Empirical formulas for predicting the maximum wave height and maximum run-up height for the RongSong (RS) landslide deposit at the RM Hydropower Station are developed. The results highlight the potential for more concentrated energy and greater destructive power in landslide-generated waves in mountainous reservoirs compared to those in open water areas.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most destructive natural hazards, causing substantial loss of life and infrastructure, particularly in mountainous regions. Accurate identification of landslide-prone areas remains challenging due to complex and nonlinear interactions among geological, topographical, and environmental factors. This study evaluates kernel-based machine learning approaches, namely, kernel logistic regression (KLR) and support vector machine (SVM), for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) in Sikkim, India. A balanced data set comprising 693 landslide and 695 nonlandslide samples was constructed using 15 conditioning factors representing topographic, hydrological, environmental, geological, and seismic conditions. The grid search method was utilized to identify optimal hyperparameter configurations. Model performance was quantitatively assessed using accuracy, kappa coefficient, specificity, area under curve (AUC), landslide density, and success rate curve (SRC). The results demonstrate that the KLR with a polynomial kernel (KLR_poly) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.741 and an area under curve (AUC) of 0.829, outperforming other KLR variants, while the SVM with an rbf kernel (SVM_rbf) achieved the highest predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.749 and an AUC of 0.764, outperforming other SVM variants. Furthermore, the landslide density analysis showed a systematic increase in landslide concentration from low to high susceptibility classes for nonlinear models, while SRC results indicated moderate to good predictive capability across all models, confirming effective spatial prioritization of landslide-prone areas. Additionally, a feature importance analysis was conducted to identify the most significant factors influencing landslide occurrence.

Accurate identification and delineation of individual landslides remain challenging because of scale variation, irregular morphology, and interference from visually similar backgrounds in complex mountainous terrain. To address these challenges, we modified Mask R-CNN’s feature pathway and mask supervision. ResNet50 was replaced with SwinV2-Tiny for hierarchical feature extraction, while the feature pyramid network (FPN) was retained for multi-scale fusion. Spatially adaptive feature modulation (SAFM) was applied after the FPN to adjust spatial responses using local features and broader context. Binary cross-entropy (BCE) and Dice losses were combined to supervise pixel-wise foreground–background discrimination and instance-mask overlap. A curated dataset combining imagery from Bijie, the Diverse Mountainous Landslide Dataset (DMLD), and ScienceDB was used for training, validation, and internal testing. All configurations were evaluated using the Common Objects in Context (COCO) instance-mask protocol. Across three training seeds, SwinV2–FPN–SAFM Mask R-CNN achieved an internal test average precision (AP0.50:0.95) of 0.6158±0.0082 (mean ± sample standard deviation). Its mean mask AP0.50:0.95 exceeded those of ResNet50–FPN Mask R-CNN and Mask2Former–Swin-T by 6.21 and 3.51 percentage points, respectively. It achieved the highest mean mask AP0.50:0.95 among the ten evaluated configurations. papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are common geological disasters that cause extensive damage and significant harm. Efficient recognition of landslide remote sensing images holds both theoretical and practical importance. However, practical landslide detection faces challenges including limited data, high computation, large memory use, and low accuracy. In this study, high-quality landslide remote sensing images were collected from southeastern Xizang to construct a landslide remote sensing data set. To address the issue of insufficient samples, an improved model, landslide-deep convolutional generative adversarial network (L-DCGAN), based on DCGAN, was proposed to enhance landslide remote sensing data. The enhanced data set was constructed by incorporating efficient channel attention (ECA) and squeeze-and-excitation (SE) modules into the generator and discriminator, respectively. Additionally, an improved YOLOv8 model, landslide-you only look once version 8(L-YOLOv8), was proposed. First, the cross-stage partial pyramid convolution (CSPPC) and grouped and shuffled convolution (GSConv) modules replaced the cross stage partial layer with 2 branches (C2f) module and ordinary convolution in the network to reduce the number of model parameters and computational complexity. Then, the spatial and channel synergistic attention (SCSA) mechanism was introduced to improve detection accuracy. Experimental results showed that compared with the original YOLOv8 algorithm, the number of model parameters in L-YOLOv8 was reduced by approximately 41.78%, and the average accuracy on the landslide sample data set was increased by 0.57%, and frames per second (FPS) was improved by 33.87%. The model achieved lightweight design while improving detection speed and accuracy, and demonstrated superior performance on the landslide remote sensing data set.

papers.summary: Abstract Heavy rainfall is a common natural phenomenon. Regarding the issue of water infiltration in an infinite vegetated slope (consisting of rooted and unrooted layers) under the heavy rainfall condition, the infiltration process is divided into two stages— before and after the slope surface reaches saturation—and the corresponding analytical solutions are acquired through several mathematical approaches. Then the proposed solutions are effectively verified by two comparisons. Finally, based on the factor of safety ( F s ), the effects of key factors on the slope’s shallow stability are quantitatively investigated, and some novel findings are obtained. For example, an increased heavy rainfall rate reduces the F s , but this effect exhibits a tendency of increasing and then decreasing. An increase in transpiration rate enhances the infinite vegetated slope’s whole stability, while its influence will be declined after the heavy rainfall infiltration. The increased root tensile strength improves the F s within the rooted layer, but does not affect the unrooted layer’s stability. Moreover, compared with the “exponential” root shape, the F s within the unrooted layer is slightly lower in the case of the “uniform” root shape. Overall, the findings provide useful insights into infiltration mechanisms and shallow stability of infinite vegetated slopes under heavy rainfalls.

papers.summary: Abstract The soil layer up to a certain depth below the ground surface exists in an unsaturated state, where factors such as precipitation, evaporation, and prolonged subsurface heat waves control the state and material properties of soil. The suction stress that contributes to the resistance of the soil mass governs the stability of geostructures and depends on the thermal and hydraulic interactions in unsaturated soil. No solutions are available to determine the suction stress in soils subjected to transient flow conditions at elevated temperatures. This study develops closed-form expressions for temperature-dependent suction stress under transient flow conditions using the one-dimensional transient flow equation and a temperature-dependent soil–water retention curve. The developed equation was implemented within the framework of stress-based finite-element limit analysis to evaluate the stability of strip plate anchors in terms of their uplift capacity embedded in unsaturated sand, silt, and clay under transient flow conditions and varying temperatures. The critical role of thermal and hydraulic interactions in different types of unsaturated soils (clay, silt, and sand), specifically regarding matric suction, effective degree of saturation, and suction stress over time, has been discussed in detail. Additionally, a comprehensive parametric study has been conducted to evaluate the effects of transient flow and elevated temperature on the uplift capacity of shallow strip plate anchors. The results indicate that the behavior of plate anchors in unsaturated sand and silt is distinctly different from that in clay.

papers.summary: ABSTRACT This study evaluates andesite rock slope stability in İzmir, Türkiye, using mobile LiDAR (iPhone 14Pro) and hybrid classification systems. The acquired 3D point cloud (1.7 × 106 points) demonstrated high spatial accuracy when validated against global navigation satellite system data. Automated analysis via discontinuity set extractor revealed that applying a “full-persistence” assumption artificially reduces mean discontinuity spacing by 40–70 percent compared with a realistic “non-persistence” model, drastically underestimating rock block sizes. Kinematic analysis indicated a 40 percent probability of wedge failure, primarily driven by the highly persistent J6 set (lmax = 16 m). To directly compare slope mass rating (SMR), Q-slope, and rock hazard index (RHI) outputs, a “normalized risk index (Rindex)” was utilized. SMR yielded an overly optimistic evaluation Rindex = 0.41, failing to capture the geometric severity of the critical wedge. In contrast, RHI successfully identified this localized hazard (“moderate risk,” Rindex = 0.51) by directly accounting for geometric continuity. The Q-slope system proved to be the most conservative (Rindex = 0.60), indicating that the current 72° slope requires a reduction to 57°. The findings demonstrate that integrating mobile LiDAR with geometry-sensitive systems such as RHI provides a more reliable, targeted hazard assessment than traditional approaches.

papers.summary: Abstract The paper focuses on the effect of the vertical ground acceleration component on slope stability. The proposed stability method is based on Newmark’s sliding block concept, which provides an intuitive indicator of slope stability. Contrary to the original Newmark method, both components of excitations, tangent and normal to the slip plane, are considered in force equilibrium. In the paper, the extended Newmark method is coupled with dynamic response obtained using the FEM and a direct time-integration scheme. Coupling the simple stability approach with the stress distribution history eliminates uncertainty in determining the intensity of the dynamic load acting on the sliding block. In the coupled method, the equilibrium of the sliding and resisting forces is considered along the discretized slip plane. When the limit equilibrium is reached, the relative movement of the block begins, and the permanent displacement of a sliding mass is accumulated. The influence of excitation components on permanent displacement is examined using a uniform steep slope as an example. The presented results indicate that shallow deformation mechanisms are more strongly affected by inertial forces than deeper ones. In the analyzed cases, the peak average acceleration for the shallow mechanism was between 1.2 and 3.0 times that for the deep mechanism. Furthermore, the effect of vertical acceleration on permanent displacements is notably more significant in shallow failure modes. It is shown that the permanent displacement obtained by the original Newmark’s method can be 74.3% lower than that obtained by the extended Newmark’s method. The impact of vertical acceleration itself can reach 24.6%.

papers.summary: Abstract Landslides are among the most significant natural hazards in the Himalayan region of India, causing substantial damage to infrastructure, natural resources, and local communities. This study presents an integrated hydro-geotechnical approach for regional landslide susceptibility assessment by combining statistical susceptibility mapping with slope stability evaluation. The proposed framework considers the influence of key hydrologic factors, including rainfall, drainage density, topographic wetness, and groundwater conditions, together with geotechnical properties to better explain the mechanisms controlling slope failure. Five bivariate statistical models, namely, frequency ratio (FR), information value (IV), weight of evidence (WoE), certainty factor (CF), and Shannon entropy (SE), were applied to produce landslide susceptibility maps. Their performance was evaluated using the area under the curve (AUC) and landslide density index (LDI). Among the evaluated models, SE achieved the highest predictive accuracy ( AUC = 87.17 % ), followed closely by FR (87.06%). The results indicate that steep slopes ( > 30 ° ), weak lithological formations, high drainage density, and groundwater conditions are the main factors controlling landslide occurrence in the study area. Slope stability was further evaluated using laboratory-derived geotechnical parameters and circular failure charts (CFC), providing an independent assessment of slope conditions under different groundwater scenarios. The combined use of statistical modeling, hydrologic factors, and geotechnical verification improves the reliability of landslide susceptibility assessment and provides a practical framework that can be applied in other mountainous regions affected by rainfall-induced landslides.

papers.summary: Regional Landslide Early Warning Systems (LEWS) are essential tools for predicting rainfall-induced slope instability across broad geographic regions. This thesis provides an evaluation of the regional LEWS in Catalonia, Spain, assessing its real-time operational performance and sensitivity across operational factors (2024–2025) and its forecast reliability across 24 h and 48 h predictive lead times (2024–2026). papers.title: Development of an AI-Driven Model to Predict Slope Collapse Due to Rainfall
papers.summary: Rainfall-induced slope instability is one of the most critical geotechnical hazards worldwide, causing significant damage to infrastructure and loss of life. Predicting slope stability under rainfall conditions remains challenging due to the complex interaction between soil properties, slope geometry, and transient hydrological processes. This research addresses this challenge by developing a reliable and practical predictive framework that integrates experimental investigation, numerical modeling, and machine learning. The study was conducted in three sequential stages. First, geotechnical centrifuge tests were performed at the University of Western Ontario to investigate slope response under controlled rainfall conditions. A calibrated rainfall simulation system ensured uniform and repeatable rainfall application, while slope deformation and pore water pressures were monitored to understand failure mechanisms. Second, numerical simulations using SEEP/W and SLOPE/W were conducted to evaluate slope stability across a wide range of conditions, including different soil types (clay, silt, and sand), slope geometries, and rainfall scenarios. This process generated a comprehensive dataset of 21,438 cases. Finally, machine learning models, including Multiple Linear Regression, Random Forest, and Extra Trees, were developed to predict the factor of safety using seven input variables. The Extra Trees model showed the highest predictive accuracy and strong generalization capability, particularly under unseen slope geometries. The results also highlight the importance of including rainfall intensity and duration in predictive models. The developed model was implemented into a web-based early warning system capable of providing rapid predictions. This research contributes to improved hazard assessment and supports the development of practical tools for geotechnical risk mitigation.

papers.title: Base-level lowering rates control a landslide process transition in California's Franciscan mélange
papers.summary: California’s Franciscan mélange is well-known for hosting persistent, slow-moving earthflows, a landslide style favored by the unit’s significant local variability in shear strength (e.g. Medley, 2001; Kim et al., 2004; Roering et al., 2015). Big Sur’s mélange, however, is unusual: landslide mapping there reveals both recent (e.g. the 2017 Mud Creek landslide) and prehistoric rotational landslides on slopes that are unusually steep for this lithology. Because rotational landslides and earthflows pose markedly different hazards, understanding what drives the shift in failure style is critical for hazard assessment. Here we test the hypothesis that the rate of base-level lowering governs the transition between earthflow and rotational failure. We synthesize landslide mapping and analysis of high-resolution topography across two Franciscan mélange settings with contrasting rates of base-level lowering: the South Fork Eel River canyon, where river incision drives base-level lowering at ~1 mm/yr, and the southern Big Sur coast, where wave erosion drives local base-level lowering at ~2 cm/yr. We then use 2-D numerical modeling to test whether rapid coastal retreat alone can drive a transition from earthflow to rotational failure in a Franciscan mélange hillslope.Landslide mapping shows that landslide activity in Big Sur, as defined by InSAR-derived deformation rates, is concentrated along the actively eroding coastline, and that the two regions differ systematically in failure style according to overall hillslope angle. Big Sur’s steeper slopes are dominated by rotational landslides, while the Eel River region’s shallower slopes are dominated by earthflows. Numerical modeling shows that progressive lateral erosion can produce rotational failure on hillslopes that were previously deforming as earthflows, provided there is some degree of vertical heterogeneity in the weathering profile. papers.title: Digital soil mapping of mountain soils: from pedodiversity to land vocation and ecosystem services
papers.source: AMS Dottorato Institutional Doctoral Theses Repository (University of Bologna)
papers.summary: This doctoral research explored the application of Geographic Information System (GIS) and Digital Soil Mapping (DSM) techniques to improve soil mapping processes and support land management and biodiversity conservation, in alignment with the objectives of the National Biodiversity Future Center (NBFC). The study was conducted in two Regional Parks of the Northern Apennines, a region characterized by high environmental heterogeneity and a rich cartographic heritage. Traditional pedological knowledge and expert-driven selection of environmental covariates were first employed to delineate land units and produce a conventional soil map. Subsequently, DSM approaches using Random Forest models with recursive feature elimination were applied to generate an alternative soil map based on DEM derivatives and remotely sensed data, achieving high accuracy and interpretability. The analysis identified key drivers of soil differentiation, such as topography, insolation, vegetation indices, and proximity to water bodies, highlighting their potential for transferability to similar areas and for overcoming cartographic discontinuities. Complementary studies on the same area revealed that climate exerts a stronger influence than vegetation on soil evolution, and that considering soil diversity enhances understanding of organic matter dynamics. The second component of this research addressed the reestablishment of chestnut cultivation in the Northern Apennines through a land suitability model that was tested on the municipality of Castel del Rio (BO). The resulting map identified both underutilized suitable lands and cultivated areas with significant limitations, findings that were corroborated by the severe landslides of May 2023. Moreover, the study suggested that land morphology and soil characteristics may influence the spread of ink disease, a major threat to chestnut groves. papers.title: Analisis Kerawanan Longsorlahan di Kabupaten Wonogiri Berdasarkan Sistem Informasi Geografis
papers.source: UMS Library Center of Academic Activities (Universitas Surakarta)
authors: , Dr. Annisa Trisnia Sasmi, S.Si., M.T
papers.summary: Landslides are processes involving the downslope movement of soil and/or rock masses due to slope instability. Wonogiri Regency exhibits diverse topographic, rainfall, geological, land-use, and soil characteristics, resulting in varying levels of landslide susceptibility across the region. This study aims to analyze the spatial distribution of landslide susceptibility levels and their correspondence with actual landslide occurrences in Wonogiri Regency. A quantitative method was employed using a Geographic Information System (GIS) approach via the Weighted Overlay method. The parameters utilized included rainfall, slope gradient, geology, land use, and soil type. Each parameter was assigned a score and weight, followed by an overlay process to generate a landslide susceptibility map. Validation was conducted using 85 landslide occurrence points from 2025, obtained from the Wonogiri Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency (BPBD), with 12 of these points verified through field surveys. The results indicate that landslide susceptibility is categorized into four classes: low, moderate, high, and very high. The moderate susceptibility class covers the largest area. Validation results show that 57 occurrence points (67.06%) fall within the high susceptibility class, while 28 points (32.94%) fall within the moderate susceptibility class; no occurrence points were found in the low susceptibility class. These findings demonstrate that actual landslides occurred more frequently in areas classified as having high susceptibility compared to those with moderate susceptibility.

papers.title: INTEGRASI PERSISTENT SCATTERER INTERFEROMETRIC SYNTHETIC APERTURE RADAR (PS-INSAR) DAN ANALYTICAL HIERARCHY PROCESS (AHP) UNTUK PEMETAAN KERAWANAN LONGSOR DI SEKITAR LAPANGAN PANAS BUMI WAYANG WINDU
papers.source: Repository at Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia (Universitas Pendidikan Indonesia)
papers.summary: Kawasan Panas Bumi Wayang Windu merupakan wilayah yang memiliki potensi tanah longsor yang tinggi. Pemetaan kerawanan longsor umumnya masih menggunakan parameter statis sehingga belum sepenuhnya merepresentasikan kondisi pergerakan permukaan tanah secara aktual. Pembobotan parameter dilakukan menggunakan AHP berdasarkan penilaian ahli, kemudian seluruh parameter diintegrasikan melalui analisis weighted overlay. papers.title: Advances in the detection and monitoring of mass-movement processes through high-resolution remote sensing data
papers.summary: With advances in satellite technology, spaceborne data are becoming available to the public and scientific community at increasing temporal and spatial resolutions. These data open new opportunities to study Earth-surface processes in unprecedented detail. This thesis investigates the potential and challenges of high-resolution optical data for monitoring slow-moving landslides and the generation of digital elevation models (DEMs) to improve subsequent topographic analyses. The study area is set in the northwest Argentinean Andes -- a region particularly susceptible to mass movement processes due to steep topography, heavy rainfall during the summer monsoon, and geologic pre-conditioning. GNSS field measurements were employed to validate the derived elevations and identify optimal processing parameters. papers.title: Multi-hazard modelling of hydro-geomorphological events for early warning systems. Application to the Val d’Aran (Central Pyrenees, Spain)
papers.summary: (English) Hydro-geomorphological hazards such as floods and rainfall-induced landslides frequently co-occur in mountainous regions, driven by shared meteorological forcing but governed by distinct hydrological and geotechnical mechanisms. The research progresses through three interconnected stages. First, an event-based slope stability model is enhanced through a novel multi-objective calibration strategy that explicitly represents both antecedent and final slope stability conditions. Results demonstrate that inadequate representation of subsurface hydrological states leads to physically inconsistent pre-event instability, highlighting the sensitivity of slope response to antecedent moisture conditions. papers.title: Engineering geological properties of the Awhitu Group sands at Muriwai, New Zealand
papers.summary: Landslides are a critical risk to New Zealand’s infrastructure and economy, as evidenced during the widespread early 2023 storms. The Awhitu Group sands are late Pliocene to early Pleistocene dune sands and associated facies found throughout the New Zealand North Island west coast. Muriwai, a settlement in the Auckland region, has an 80 m escarpment consisting of Awhitu Group sands that failed as fatal landslides during strong rainfall in early 2023 and in 1965. Interestingly, there is currently limited research on the geotechnical properties of the Awhitu Group sands, particularly at Muriwai. Therefore, this study aims to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the engineering geology properties of the Muriwai Awhitu Group sands to gain more appreciation for the complexity of this geological unit and the Muriwai slope conditions. papers.summary: (English) The top layer of soil on a slope is highly dynamic, influenced by atmospheric forces and the presence of vegetation.
